summary: Dynamic and Challenging Role with Room for Improvement in Work-Life Balance
pros:
Innovative Environment: Working at Santander offers the opportunity to be at the forefront of financial technology. The company places a strong emphasis on innovation, allowing for creative problem solving and the implementation of cutting-edge solutions.
Professional Growth: As a Senior Product Manager, I've had access to significant professional development opportunities. The role demands strategic thinking and offers the chance to lead major projects, enhancing leadership skills and industry knowledge.
Supportive Team Culture: The team atmosphere at Santander is highly collaborative. Colleagues and management are supportive, fostering a positive work environment where everyone's contributions are valued.
Competitive Compensation: Santander offers competitive salaries and benefits, including bonuses, health insurance, and pension contributions, which reflect the company's appreciation for its employees' hard work and dedication.
cons:
Work-Life Balance: The demanding nature of the job, especially in product management, can sometimes lead to long hours and a challenging work-life balance. This aspect can be particularly pronounced during project deadlines and product launches.
Bureaucracy and Decision-Making: As with many large organizations, there can be bureaucratic hurdles that slow down decision-making processes. This sometimes hampers agility and can delay the implementation of new ideas or solutions.
Internal Communication: While the team environment is generally positive, internal communication within the larger organization can be improved. Information silos and the lack of a streamlined communication platform sometimes lead to inefficiencies.

After that you are on your own since there's never enough staff to help you. There's so many things you have to know. You are supposed to review guidelines when you are doing transaction or query for customers that you don't know how to do - meaning that if someone calls, you just have to put them on hold for about 15 minutes before you are able to help them as guild lines just refers you to different page etc. Systems are slow and old, and glitch all the time so when customer calls it won't load their information and you can't proceed with transactions. Branches are understaffed and you are expected to take on responsibilities of private bankers without any pay rise. I don't know how about other branches, but our building was old and plumbing was always broken. We only had tap water offered and the building was always cold as they didn't want to fix the heating issues. After four o'clock they turn of heating(it's turn off my central) so you sit there in cold. We had old chairs, some of them without back rests, and they weren't adjustable. Screens are glitching. We were sharing headphones - you don't get your own. I'm counter, you don't get to use money counting machine - branch is allowed to have only one and that is in the back - so if someone asks for large amount of money or they want to deposit them, you have to manually count them. It would be much faster and there would be much less mistakes done if we would get at least one between two colleagues but they just say we can't have one - customers will look at you like idiots when you count all that money just manually.After probation you get lots of extra responsibilities for no extra pay. Pay itself is very little over the minimal wage. They expect you to come earlier to open the branch and you need to work Saturdays. I was told it's only every other but I'd worked sometimes three times in a row Saturdays. There's lots of micromanagement. You have pointless meetings that you need to put I'm writing - there's about three meetings a week amd it completely insipid. They are listening to your calls and sometimes do tests calls when someone is pretending to be customer and they pick up on tiniest things. Management is completely useless. All they do is making presentations for meetings. Lastly, you need to be offering products to customers - something they won't tell you on the interview - and they measure you against your scores. Lots of times I was left on counter on my own and I was still expected to be offering products to customers even though there were customers lined to the door. If you don't offer enough products you won't get your promised bonus.

summary: Don't let the company name fool you.
advice: Management needs to be looked into, there is far too many floor managers who know absolutely nothing and their attitudes towards they're staff members is appalling. The work atmosphere is horrendous people are humans not robots.
pros:
- Met some lovely people
- Fortunate to have been placed on the right teams with good managers
- Good with holiday pay/sick pay 
- Money is good for part time.
cons:
Everybody thinks that because Santander is a big bank that the company is good to work for.. Wrong. I worked as a customer service advisor, I worked there for nearly 2 years. 
Applying for the job is such a long process, 
Training is 4 weeks classroom based which by the way you learn absolute nothing.
You have floorwalkers who are supposed to be there to help you but huff and puff if you ask them a question or look at you like you're stupid. 
There are multiple managers on the floor no matter what time your shift is, yet you find yourself pacing up and down to find a manager because near enough every one of them refuse to take an escalation & tell you to find someone else. 
Csm's & managers are very pally between either other and talk about colleagues who work there, not very professional.
It worked out not much difference in  the pay if you worked part time rather than full time.
Managers are constantly on your case, moaning if you take an extra toilet break through your day but will only give you two 10 minute breaks for a 5 & a half hour shift so they expect you to be on the phone for 5 hours & 10 minutes straight.
Such a malicious enviroment, everyone is always gossiping about someone else who works there. 
The job itself is mentally draining, be prepared for the anxitey to kick in & the way customers speak on the phone to you is not worth the pay you get nor the stress it brings. 
Only really room for progression is if you're mates with the management not really about how well you work/how much you know.

advice:
1. Only hire front line staff if there is adequate support to fulfil their mandates. Too often ambitious front line staff come in with great ideas only to be told they can't do the things they came in to do. 
2. Reduce bureaucracy. I am ok for Madrid HQ to be involved but you might as well give an ipad to a monkey. Clueless. 
3. Clear and robust procedures. All units to work effectively together. 
4. Pay close attention to those that have been with the organisation for more than 10 years. Loyalty is one thing but apathy is another. Sometimes it's easier to coast than take a risk and go somewhere to bring new ideas. The worst thing is if someone is institutionalised and says "well that's just how things work here". There's many dinosaurs here.
pros:
1. Salary package is above market. They will recruit top talent and pay relatively well for you to build better practices
2. Autonomy and flexibility. Be ready to roll your sleeves up. You'll get a lot of autonomy to grow provided you do not interact with Madrid HQ and Credit.
3. Generally relaxed working lifestyle.
4. Some excellent people in the team. 
5. It's small so communication is easier.
cons:
1. Sub tier investment banking unit. You're not going to cut your cloth here for anything innovative. They talk it. But they don't do it.
2. Madrid HQ. Bureaucratic, unwieldy, political. It's a circus of monkeys. You're likely to come across one bright spark out of a thousand. Utter dross.
3. Shambolic at times. Your area might be purring like a Ferrari but other related areas look more like a clapped out Morris Minor. As such, you're never at the races.
4. Frustrating. See above. You'll feel like treading water and a sense of deja vu. 
5. You'll never really grow because you're not surrounded by the best people who will challenge you. Santander is like a Nokia handset to the smartphone world.

advice: Santander UK prefers to hire external workers than to promote from within. There is no incentive to improve or do better for employees as there is no reward after all your hard work and external hires always get the new positions.
pros: Location. Some incentives are good.
cons:
9 years in the same role despite trying to move to other departments or to get a promotion. After several courses and studies paid with my own salary no reward or effort was made from line managers. 
Work overtime every day but never rewarded for it.
Spanish management get top jobs whether they deserve it or not. No meritocracy. Stagnant salary over the past 4 years. Meagre bonus. There's a culture of favouritism that is hard to believe in this day and age.

summary: Overall a decent place to work
advice: Generally pleased with management. Quite a few agents express interest in moving onto mortgage advice, you have a large talent pool that isn't being tapped.
pros: Lots of support, friendly atmosphere, decent benefit package. As far as call centre work goes about as good as it gets. Clear structure & well managed. Once you get the knowledge down it is a genuinely enjoyable job, I honestly don't mind going to work everyday.
cons: Steep learning curve to begin with, progression opportunities limited to management/corporate roles. Wage slightly lower than comparable jobs in the area.

advice: Keep up the good work. The support of you all is brilliant and I love that you push us all and encourage us wherever we want to go
pros: The U.K. contact centres aren’t like other call centres, the support and environment is so warm and welcoming. Everybody is encouraged to work together as a team and pushed (in a good way) to achieving their full potential
cons: The shifts can be a bit annoying and the cafe closes at 4 pm so those working night shifts don’t have access to them

advice: As a customer service adviser you take constant back to back calls from often very unhappy customers. Your stats are monitored constantly and going to the toilet outside of your break time is a big no. They give you plenty of holidays but there's never any availability to book them so you end up losing them, having random days off here and there or if you're lucky you may get 3 days off in a row mid February... The shift pattern gives you no work life balance as you work most evenings and weekends.
pros:
Good staff 
Management is ok
cons:
Holidays 
Shift Pattern 
Customers

location: Bradford, Yorkshire and the Humber, England
advice: Please carry on the work and the speed in which things are done as & when "normality" resume's. This crisis has shown our greatest assets are our people so please continue to listen to them.
pros:
During my time at Santander lots has changed but you get a feeling that this is being done for the right reasons and I have been supported through these. The advice, help and support they have given during Covid-19 has been fantastic. This has meant I've been able to balance my work and home life better than I thought. I have been able to support my children with school work and my partner with balancing their work load as well. The company is really looking at how best to support and update us through an extremely difficult time in circumstances that change almost daily and I really feel they are putting people first.

Using platforms such as Microsoft teams, Zoom etc have really helped us to stay connected and still have that personal touch and this has been demonstrated from Exec level down.

The well-being of our people seems to be real priority now and its welcomed.

Whilst there is sadly lots of things happening in the world currently, the support we are receiving and the support we are giving our customers , really does make me feel proud to work here.
cons:
At times if there is an easy way to do something, we will find the opposite more challenging way to do it. Covid has shown we can do things quickly and its a shame it has taken such an event to accelerate some of these practices.

We still have lots of processes and policies (as you would expect in a highly legislated sector) which could be simpler but I know these are being worked on.

pros: Interesting when first joining as with any new job. Working remotely is nice. Managers are good people who seem to genuinely care about you. Targets aren't as bad as some also 'call centre' jobs. Good job stability in the current climate.
cons: No progression. Work can be depressing, dealing with angry customers on a daily basis who often blame you for going overdrawn. Very corporate feel even when working from home, making it hard to feel relaxed. Wage should be higher for what the job actually entails, can be brutal at times. So many processes you must stick to, it's hard to keep up.

summary: Your experience depends on your manager
advice: When hiring internally hire people on their merits & ability to do the job they are interviewing for not their ability to do the job they are in at the moment. Said person could be an average 'cashier' or 'Salesman' but excel in leading a team.
pros:
In the more corporate side progression can be quick
People knock it but the learning is very good, Santander as a company take responsibility for training it staff
cons: People who are good at sales or hitting targets are promoted to management, not the people who are actually good at dealing with people or a team

pros: It used to be fun and enjoyable. Since covid it's changed dramatically
cons: Worked for the company for 8 years. No progression, Salary is below average, overworked every single day and now on top of 'PB' role we are made to man the call centre lines which is awful as customers are always complaining about wait times etc. Not enough staff, poorly managed and bad communication. So many staff have left because of this and they won't change they don't care about staff anymore we are simply numbers now. Micro managed etc.

summary: A good job, a poor career choice
advice: Pay more attention to the people actually doing the job in the call center, their job makes sure you have one to do so don't treat them as inferior.
pros: Colleagues are a great laugh and support each other very much. Good incentives. Good wage for a day-to-day job.
cons: Customers are mentally numbing and depressing. Company concentrates too heavily on statistics. Every single little mistake is scrutinized. Management for the most part are ignorant of their position and act above everyone else in the office.

summary: If you are a great self starter and independent , the role is suited well as an on call customer advisor
advice: Get to know new members of your team and create a personal plan to attend to the members of starts needs and development rather than letting them just get on with the job.
pros: online training is provided for compliance and regulations, security, and overall job role for the company
cons: There was no personal or group training support outside of the online training which you were left to do in a room.

advice: Think of employees more as people to be retained and rewarded. Actually discuss career development plans with employees instead of expecting them to take on that responsibility themselves especially when top down communication is not very clear.
pros:
- High value work
- Feel like your work is actually valuable to society 
- Good colleagues that are generally supportive
- Good environment when working in office
cons:
- Old systems means you are trying to keep up with new era of granular data with clunky data
- Unclear career development paths

summary: Hard culture, not very flexible with families, but well run
advice: The obsession with cost:income ratio leads to dumb decisions.
pros: Well run (financially) company that makes it clear what constitutes success. Development opportunities are plentiful and you can make a difference.
cons: Bosses not very good with flexible working and family. Expected to work long hours, regardless of what's going on. Real 'boys' culture, aggressive and sales/numbers led. Not much intellectual leadership - graft is valued over brains. Very difficult to advance unless you get put into the talent pool by your leader.

advice: Make employees aware what is needed to do to make it to top management, having internal promotions first before looking for outsiders, have more planning and stick to it. Solving problems instead of create problems.
pros: Good job flexibility, plenty of freedom, ok work load, development in skills are fine, friendly environment, nice people around you,
cons: poor progression route, work load un-ordered, too many adhoc request, problems are being left and not solved, senior managers stays at status quo without improvement, top boss are not serious at things, not profressional enough

advice: They should prompt branch ma annagers to discuss with the rest of the people of the branch about career progression. Managers just want you to succeed in your target
pros: Nice people. Leading in the sector. They give you a good training. You will be working in a challenging environment. Efficient system.
cons: Progression within the company can be a bit slow if you start in a sales role in a branch. Salary is not great. Though comissions can be a bit better if you can get them

advice: Get up to date with employee /employment rights and listen to the back bone of the business .... your staff !!!
pros: Pay is ok .
cons: Annualised hours added to your 35 hours which are not paid for months later if you're still employed , constant threats and extension of probation absolutely no employee relationship. Training is poor with live system accounts used for training . Calls are failed due to a missed word or action  3 fails and you are out the door . Probation reviews and extensions are the bullying tactics they uses . Would not recommend anybody work in the call centre it's a disgrace with dinosaurs as managers that are nothing more than social drop outs

advice: Provide better training opportunities to staff to enable them to progress to the jobs on offer. Provide permanent contract after probationary period. You can still dismiss people within 2 years no questions asked. Lack of permanent contact causes too much uncertainty and financial limitations (e.g. mortgage).
pros:
A lot of policies to protect staff
Benefits (gym passes, discounts etc.)
Quite calm environment
cons:
Incredibly dull work
Temporary contract for 2 years
Lack of upward mobility
Unable to develop any skills outside of data entry
2 year waiting list for parking
Managers are not leaders

summary: Well looked after although training is lacking
advice: Maybe an interactive cashier training tool would be better with testing until talk’s was completed correctly
pros: Excellent benefits and you are encouraged to do well by recording your own strengths and weaknesses and they are quite flexible with childcare etc .
cons: Initial training on joining in my case was a bit lacking ,my branch was a busy branch and it was left to the other already busy cashiers to train me hence I learnt by my mistakes in a lot of cases

advice: By the time I had left, the working environment was so poor that it would take a lot to change the negative atmosphere in there. The floor manager should really make an effort with the advisors and team managers and listen to their feedback. Feedback was continuously met with the response "Well it's not going to change so deal with it."
pros: Good breaks: 1 hour unpaid, 2 x 15 minutes paid. Good onsite facilities including a large canteen and a Costa.
cons:
Poor pay and very few opportunities to ever progress. 
You are very much a number not a person. The staff turnover was high as work morale was low. The job is as you would expect from a call centre, however Santander had an extremely negative working environment as a result of poor management at levels above team managers.

summary: A considerate and ethical company to work for.
advice: Don't overlook the value that your core workers add, not everyone operates at a highly visible strategic level.  Senior Managers only two levels above me did not understand what I did or the value I added to the team.
pros:
- Large employer with many opportunities to progress.
- Excellent teamwork and (mainly) collaborative working.
- Good Head Office facilities.
- Fantastic people to work with.
cons:
- Often too many stakeholders to make quick decisions & progress.
- Very flat management structure - fewer opportunities to progress upwards.
- Some head office locations are difficult to reach by public transport.
- High expectations without the package to match.

summary: Extremely political, poor technology resourses, smart colleagues
advice:
Empower the teams to make decisions or at least involve them in decisions taken at the high-level of the bank.
Provide any kind training to recently employed people.
pros:
Great Opportunity to learn, everyone pushes you to your best.
Salary is slightly above market rates.
cons:
Extremely Political and very dependant on Madrid's HQ.
Pool technology resources: Old and Slow computers, 10-year old mouses & keyboard, terrible chairs.
None has the inclination to help you with your work, apart from giving zero training when you start.
Face-timing, the environment is that if your boss is still at the office, you should not leave. Forget about leaving anytime before 8:00PM.

summary: Good graduate scheme and a nice place to work.
advice: Providing more flexibility in rotation options for graduates would be beneficial for the business.
pros: Great graduate scheme with a good starting salary. Lot's of exposure to the different tech departments, and lot's of responsiblity is given to graduates from the start. With plenty of interesting projects using the latest tech, it was a highly motivating environment.
cons: Some graduates found it difficult to get placed in the rotations they wanted. There was also a quite a large variation in the projects, it was important to reach your preferred department in advance if you wanted to have a placement there.

location: Bradford, Yorkshire and the Humber, England
advice: Not enough space in this box.
pros: Very few (I must add five words so this is a few more)
cons: Extremely poor staff morale, Management are miss guided, systems are unconnected and investment is lacking in all areas. Complaints management and issue resolution is woefully poor. Disconnected company structure based on a culture of internal "external" outsourcing, for example IT team is actually treated as a 3rd party endeavor not an internal team. Extremely blame driven culture and incompetent senior management. Company is seen as a success due to not seemingly being affected by the credit crunch, this is actually born only from Spanish banking laws preventing the company from entering into the sub prime credit market in my opinion. Non existent career progressing proven in the fact that the HR team is woefully lacking.

advice: I would suggest a different strategy when placing managerial staff. I'd also suggest a less strict atmosphere so that employees do not feel so controlled and under pressure.
pros: Training was provided for the job. The trainers and team were lovely people who would help however they can in order to help you reach targets or with any queries.
cons: Very strict, was not allowed to listen to music whilst working (even with earphones) or speak with your colleagues. Had to make a note of everything you were doing at every moment - that includes even if you were going to the toilet.

advice: Find out what is actually grieving your staff and do something about it rather than say that's just the way it is because it isn't..
pros: Starting to consider work life balance, relatively easy, not as target driven as before and are starting to focus on the customers
cons: They expect everybody to start 15 minutes before shift due and you can finish potentially hours after end of shift and this is expected depending on role. Mainly late issue for cashiers. Difficult to get any time back. Poor management level pay generally means poor management.  Due to branch reduction plans limited career opportunities.

summary: Great friendly staff. Underpaid, Lack of Communication
advice: Change the dress code. Modernise it up and make it casual dress all the time, as we are a non customer facing role. Listen to negative feedback and don't shoot down when voicing concerns or opinions
pros:
Most staff are very friendly. 
Dress down Friday
cons:
Underpaid for being a specialist department. 
They say we should speak up and voice our concerns, however when this is done mostly we are told that we are speaking out of turn, as its truths they do not want to hear.
Pays a lot less than other banks
The dress code on non dress down days is archaic

advice: Continue being helpful!
pros: Fellow employees at Santander we're friendly and approachable especially when i was dealing with any challenges as a new joiner.
cons: I was promised that career progression within my role in the company would be available  but found that to be false the longer i stayed at Santander.  There where opportunities within the company on an internal job board but in terms of progression within my specific role it was severely limited. having to wait for a manager to leave before being able to progress as one was frustrating as i had moved over from a previous job as a manager.

advice: To make a more equitable system based on experience rather than personal feelings,
pros: Good benefits, competitive salary for the job role, okay working hours, can encounter some great people to work with, local management can be a great help with work life balance depending on who that may be.
cons: Huge amount of workplace politics, little to no room for career progression for most people, changing goal posts, yearly mass redundencies and cost cutting, vague expectations year on year with arbitary ratings given mainly on how someone feels about you, career progression often gets blocked by regional or divisional management, increased workload year on year.

advice:
Increase salaries. Barclays pay £17k per year for the same job. Some jobs will use your current salary to limit how much you can ask for
Give advisors more individual responsibility to grow as a person and gain experience to move where they want to
pros:
Flexible hours
Nice people
Twice yearly bonus is available depending on performance
Only inbound calls
No sales targets 
Fridays and weekends are dress down
cons:
Crowded work place
Lower salary than competition
Call centre work
Need to move to different cities to move to different departments
The stats needed to maintain are challenging

summary: I'm still there after nearly a decade so take from that what you will!
pros: Really good annual leave, friendly people, reasonably flexible working, culture is generally pretty good and you aren't expected to work long hours just for the sake of it (although obviously there are times when you have to)
cons:
Organisation is complex with lots of processes to navigate. Different areas don't always work together in the optimum way and there can be conflicting interests.

There's still some inconsistencies between areas (in terms of pay, bonus, perks, management, etc.)

advice: Intern/Grad Scheme organisers could be more open to department change.
pros:
Brilliant opportunities for career development and personal development.

Was placed in a small team, brilliant management, extremely enjoyable internship.
cons:
For other people the 'intern and grad scheme team' did not seem to cater for individual requests and seem to just move numbers around on a screen to sort rotations.  
However personally they placed me very well which included a call beforehand to discuss the department role and my views on working there.

summary: Nice company culture but lack of progression
advice: Explore paying employees as much as our closest competitors. Explore how to give people more opportunities to expand their career.
pros: The people are amazing and some of the nicest you could work with, they also genuinely care about customers and try to do right by them
cons: There are few options for career progression and loyalty is not rewarded. Management rely on the great company culture to retain people despite employees being paid below market rates and offered few opportunities to advance.

advice: management needs to encourage staff to move up the career ladder by creating a definitive structure and atmosphere to encourage this, so that talents are not lost to competitors
pros: friendly place to work, structured approach to staff appraisals and less focus on target but highly focused on delivering excellent customer experience
cons: the remuneration is low compared to industry standard. Also the succession plan to move up the career ladder is not well spelt out leading to demotivated staff and fairly high attrition rate.

summary: Shame they didn't keep the talent!
advice: Give people equal opportunities. Most CSM 3's that got "forced" out last year without fair opportunity was a shame. I ended up taking redundancy due to the lack of equal opportunity in the branch network.
pros: Met some of the best people over the years and some true leaders that will forever guide my path into my future.
cons: Unfortunately during the restructure they failed to retain a few of the best people that had committed their hard work & dedication over the years!

advice: Examine FCA customer outcomes and see if you are truly living up tp them. customers should come first all of the time.  Invest in older staff for advisory roles and manage turnover better.
pros: Large company, opportunity to transfer throughout the country.  Great colleagues to work with. Development of younger staff from base roles to management.
cons: Financial advisers are too young. lack of gravitas.  Management culture 1980's too many phone calls to manage underperfornancce.  High pressured sales .

advice: Present a clearer vision and strategy and live up to the company behaviours by bringing passion. Re-launching company behaviours does not in itself constitute strong leadership and a clear vision for the future direction of the company.
pros: Innovative scale challenger bank that has plenty of potential for growth in the UK. Good internal mobility if willing and able to re-locate.
cons: bureaucratic, poor leadership from the top with a lot of good senior leaders leaving. Very London-centric for senior roles. Focus on style over substance.

advice: Branch staff need to be able to be more open when upper management comes to store so they can get an insight into what it is really like, rather than what the branch want upper Management to think.
pros:
Easy to progress to branch management if you work hard.

Part time hours can be flexible.
cons:
The way the job is described at interview is very different.

As with all jobs some managers are great and some are terrible, literally ruining the lives of their staff.

location: Bradford, Yorkshire and the Humber, England
pros:
Identifying/ flagging fraudulent and unusual activity as it is essential to protecting customers and the bank.
• Using listening and questioning skills to support customer profiling
• Having the product knowledge and understanding of internal processes and procedures, good computing and numeracy skills.
• Displaying teamwork with a high level of motivation.
• Being part of a team responsible or verifying customers who have failed the first and second stage of security, requiring great judgement and responsibility.
cons: No downside of working, just to understand fast face environment

summary: The culture is destructive to both staff and customers.
advice: If staff were treated better, then customer service would improve. Having 9 behaviours, but having them mean nothing is redundant. Another box ticking exercise which serves no purpose other than to pretend Santander is a fair place to work.
pros: My team members were friendly and helpful
cons:
The role is for customer service, however the customer is never put first. 
Targets in general are too tight. 
Other departments/ colleagues refusing to take ownership. 
Nobody seems to care about the customers 
Terrible employer for people with mental health issues, there is little to no understanding.
Management cannot help with simple queries and instead direct you to teammates for help 
A 'box ticking' culture
Lack of transparency 
Terrible working hours - often scheduling you to work until 9pm one week followed directly the day after with 7am starts. Almost impossible to request holidays and even if you do so months in advance they will not schedule random days. 
A sense of feeling always replaceable and under valued for the work you do

advice: Ensure that candidates receive feedback from interviews within reasonable time frames, even if feedback is negative should still be delivered. This is is the only way a candidate can improve.
pros: Interviewers were nice and professional. I can't provide any positive feedback beyond that.
cons: My interview was scheduled for 1 hour. I spend there 1.5 hours as conversation was flying. Questions were quite intense but I answered everything with solid examples. I got impression that  I was liked and expected to get into the second round of interviews. It has been 4 months now and I they didn't even bother to provide me with feedback. I rang and emailed HR multiple times. It's clear I wasn't successful for this job however feedback should be provided no matter what. It's just disrespectful. I invested my time to get to the office on time, rearrange my day and to ensure sufficient time, I was there longer than planned, than chased multiple times for feedback and received no commentary.  No ways to improve myself if there is no feedback.

advice: Try and actually understand what it is your employees actually do, and then maybe go further and don't consistently go out of your way to make their lives more difficult
pros: My hours were only 9am-5pm with an hour lunch break; that is honestly the only positive thing that I can think of from my whole time there
cons:
- No-one in management seems to have any idea of what work is actually carried out, not a single one could perform the duties of anyone below them. They are so far disconnected from the day-to-day operations of the company that they have zero insight as to what is going on
- Guidelines and processes change on a near-constant basis with no-one being notified - no-one was ever sure of what the correct procedures for any tasks were
- Absolutely zero prospects for career progression
- Incredibly poor pay and bonus structure. Contractors will be paid up to five times more than you for doing the same work (typically to a far poorer standard)

advice: Try and improve shift patterns for call centre workers and managers, maybe with a bit more flexibility. Be transparent with people about what the job is actually like - constant queueing, call after call, high stress environment, etc during recruitment and training.
pros: Decent pay and benefits. Great training, with trainers who went out of their way to help new starts. Nice rainbow lanyards for LGBT & allies. Hour long lunches, which were great if they were at a normal lunchtime and not at 6 in the evening.
cons: Horrible hours, didn't get out of work until 9 or later most nights and very rarely had weekends off. Certain managers could be abrasive at times (although this is understandable given the pressure on them). Impossible to book any annual leave at all. High staff turnover. Ridiculous targets. Santander behaviours seemed to be all talk and no action.

summary: Positive overall, fantastic work life balance, great work culture. Salary not competitive with other banks
advice: Make base salaries in line with competitors
pros: Great place to work for and genuinely think I’ll be back there one day in the future to work. I learnt a lot working in the Transformation office under COO function (ChangeHub). Great work life balance, decent pension and benefits. Great exposure to different areas of banking if you make sure to put yourself out there. Not too formal, but very professional
cons: Only draw back was salary to be honest. Even when I got a promotion from one salary band to another, the best offer was a 5% raise on my base salary. Outside offers I received were well over 5 figures higher for similar roles. To be honest, that’s the only reason I left. Good company.

summary: Good pay but nothing else going
advice: Quit now before your sacked anyway
pros:
Good pay and benefits, 
Some nice management staff
cons: Company couldnt care less about employees, saw people that had worked there over 20 years made redundant because of a restructure. Made me realise that they expect loyalty but never show any. I ended up leaving over the inflexible hours and bully managers who had been brought over from A&L - she was a horrible little human who tried to talk down to people actually doing their jobs while she sat there and done sweet fa. We were told we would be working 1-9 shifts every 6 weeks and it ended up being every other, when in tears to management about the effect it was having on my mental health nothing was reported back and no effort to get the system changed.

advice: No advice, there’s a reason why this bank is where it is.
pros: The people. One great thing about Santander is that the people here are genuinely nice and you can get on with outside of work.
cons:
Consultancy graduate scheme that started in 2019 was poor.  Graduates were doing a level 4 apprenticeship provided by QA. The premise of the scheme wasn’t made until contracts were signed up. Some had to do Maths and English tests that a 12 year would effortlessly pass.

No sense there being an internal consultancy within a company, project managers are more likely to get real use out of experienced external consultants from the big four despite their pricing as opposed to hiring graduates who were in university 6 months prior. Grads often found themselves doing menial admin work or were isolated in London offices with whole teams being based in different parts of the UK.

Inconsistencies, grads being denied moving into full time roles where others are allowed. Unsure what this was based on .

summary: Benefits, long term job, supportive with everything
advice: Be willing to take a lot of work on and be supportive with your colleagues- you are all in this together, no matter what band or job you have, you should be treated equally at all times
pros: Great benefits, supportive business, progression, training, Great networking, very flexible hours and considerate. Long term team work colleagues, engaging with Weekly updates with what’s going on in the workplace to get involved with. A wonderful place to work
cons: Management can get caught up in a lot of things therefore not recognise the hard work that you put in as an individual and your success isn’t always highlighted and shared which can make you feel isolated and feel like the business don’t have recognition for their employees

advice: Value your staff with experience and ideas, or they will leave.
pros:
I have had many opportunities at Santander that probably would not have been available to me elsewhere.
The people working for Santander are (on the whole) warm, friendly and genuinely want to do their best.
cons:
Discrimination (when it does occur, albeit rarely) isn't take seriously.
Senior management are often unwilling to invest in staff, and when staff make suggestions about improvements it is often left to the person suggesting ideas to implement them (without support).
Your job role can change significantly over the years, meaning the job you start off in might not be the same 2-3 years down the line.
Experienced and capable staff are often the first to leave.

summary: Good to work for if you have a good team and manager
advice:
Invest in your current employees more.
Don't let great talent go wasted.
If you say you are going to do something then actually do it.
pros:
If you have a good and understanding manager it's a great place to work.
Good training resources
Can build good relationships with customers, they can be great.

location: Bradford, Yorkshire and the Humber, England
advice: Stop abiding by the rules so strictly. Understand your colleagues. Review hearings are there for people to be HEARD. There is no understanding shown by the management to the lower down colleagues, even though the majority started in these positions!
pros:
Training period is extensive and covers A LOT! You will certainly be prepared for one you go onto the floor. My training last 8 weeks, before taking a single call (all at full pay too).

Pays well for a part time role, alongside university this was a solid position. Most of my team saw this role as their ‘bit on the side’, it wasn’t really anyone’s main gig as we were mostly students.
cons:
VERY strict on their ‘policies’ and don’t seem to take into consideration other factors or show human understanding. 

For example, if you start your shift at 9am you are expected to log into your computer between 8:59 & 31 seconds and 9:00 & 29 seconds. If you log into your computer outside of these times you will get told off. I was once called into a one to one meeting with a manager for logging in EARLY by 18 seconds. The manager tried to justify this with some ‘waffle’ about how it “messes with the clock in systems which organise your pay”- which is a total lie because you’re paid salary, so doesn’t reflect this system at all. 

The shift and break times are set in bursts so you are likely never on a break with another member of your team. Understandably this is to make sure there are less advisors away from their desk at any one time, however, this makes your hour long lunch breaks often boring and lonely. Especially considering you are not allowed on your phone in the office for data protection reasons. 

Talking of the fixed breaks and lunches, the fixing of these is out of your control and are often randomly positioned. For example, I once had my ‘first break’ of 10 mins scheduled 4 hours 30 mins into my shift, I would then return to work for 20 mins before going on my hour long lunch. It’s worth noting also you are NOT allowed to go to the bathroom during your shift, you are instructed to wait until your break like you are some form of school child. Going to the bathroom is a basic human right, and everyone knows that sometimes their morning coffee can ‘go straight through’- now imagine realising you still had 4 hours until your first 10 min break because the spacing of them are so illogical! You can request to have permission to lock your computer into the ‘comfort break’ setting however you are only allowed to enter this code if permitted by a manager after presenting a medical note! As a new starter I assumed I could enter the ‘comfort break’ mode if I needed to use the bathroom but that is not the case, and the managers can see whenever you enter a new ‘code’ on your computer, and I returned to my desk to see a snooty post it note from my manager to go see her to discuss why I needed the bathroom (can’t imagine the reaction I would’ve got if I said I went for a number two!). 

You’re also expected to continue well beyond your actual shift time, despite not having any leniency whatsoever on your login times. On a late shift I was once in the call centre 1 hour and 40 minutes after the centre ‘closed’ on the exact same call. I was not paid over time for this period, or offered ‘time back’ like is often hinted should happen during training in these circumstances. I was never late for my shift during my 10 months at the company, however, having seen the storm it caused when I logged in just after 9:00:30 (still technically at 9:00 on the computers clock) I can only imagine the reaction if I arrived 1 hour 40 mins late.

Finally, more so with the policies. The probation policy and relation to sickness is complete nonsense and the reason I am no longer working at the company. In the same year I started at Santander I had a serious illness and a defective immune system, which I made clear in one of my first one to ones with my manager. I joined in June, probation was supposed to last 6 months, so by late November I was told I would be out of ‘grad bay’ and fully out of probation. I took a period of sickness in roughly August, for 2 days, I returned for one shift, and was off for the next week (5 shifts) sick. I had a doctors note as I had caught measles, as well as presumably some other viral infection. This went down as two periods of sickness despite all being covered under the same doctors note. This is essentially why I lost my job, as the probation policy states after two periods of sickness, the probation is extended for a further 3 months! In those further 3 months we go through to late February/Early March, in which I’d not taken any further days of sickness- until my sister, and her boyfriend who had recently returned from skiing in Italy and Switzerland both came down with a ‘flu’ like illness. As I’m sure you will all be aware, this was likely COVID-19, which at the time was not being tested for widely, it was only those who were hospital admissions and key NHS staff being tested. I believe that it is almost guaranteed I caught Covid-19 and took a week off, luckily for myself it was only like a cold, however my sisters boyfriend did later require a night on oxygen in a hospital! Because of this weeks sickness, I had technically had 3 periods of sickness and was called in for a ‘probation review hearing’ to see if I can continue my employment at Santander. I pleaded with my manager to not call the meeting as it was “clear and obvious that the first two sickness’ were linked, and the doctors note also covered this”, my manager agreed and said it was an impartial manager who knew nothing of the case to review this. The manager did not care for clear common sense of the link between the first two absences, or the arrival of an impending pandemic, and I was told my probation was ended with immediate effect. Thankfully, I was not sacked from my role, and officially I did “not complete probation”. I was paid gardening leave for a month, did not get to collect my belongings and was walked off the site by security (presumably other people have caused a scene). It’s worth noting that two security guards were stood at the meeting door during the whole review process, so I believe this ‘impartial’ manager had already made up his mind before even seeing the evidence. However, as far as I am concerned I should have been out of probation in November, it should never have been extended for the first two absences, and the third was literally because of a global pandemic. I left with my head held high but in shock at how little logic and human nature is shown as the rules are just interpreted black and white “you had three periods of sicknesses and this breaches the policy”.

I joined the organisation because of our purpose; 'To help people and businesses prosper' and that has never changed - it remains as engaging to me today as it did when I joined as does our values of Simple Personal and Fair. Today I'm very fortunate to do a job I truly love and does get me up in the morning and sometimes keeps me up at night (in a good way!). Our leadership and colleagues have been outstanding during the last 6 months through the Covid pandemic - showing genuine care for our colleagues and customers and its been a time of significant challenge to our business like many others, but we remain focussed on the right things going forward and are really committed to understanding how we can keep the unintended benefits that have arisen from the crisis to ensure we are a great place to work where all colleagues can be heir trues selves and thrive.
cons: Like many organisations, we have areas that we have wanted to address and improve for some time but they are not easy e.g. simplify our policies and processes, improve speed of decision making, strip out silos and work collaboratively and be more innovative in how we work. pros:

cons:
The pay still isn’t as competitive as local rivals HSBC and RBS Group, who offer more than our base salary for the same work.

Once you’re upskilled to handle calls about overdraft fees customers are incredibly abusive. We aren’t adequately prepared to deal with these customers — there’s no soft skills focus in classroom or on-the-phone training; the focus is on passing for “Risk” (Largely just following the script), which means colleagues can’t properly communicate why they can’t do something for the customer.

Our old system was garbage. Our new system isn’t finished — you can break it by not logging out the right way — but upper management decided it was ready to be used. An hour and a half of the three hours’ training we got on the new system focussed on how we could log in and out, and why it was beneficial for the business.

Managers say that Core Retail is the home of all the business’ opportunities, but experienced colleagues get overlooked for class clowns who stroke certain CSTLs’ egos. 

Some CSTLs cannot understand how a mental health issue can affect a colleague’s ability to do their job, which is frankly shocking.

The company’s corporate behaviours are there to make employees tick boxes — how they can impact your bonus and how they make you more valued isn’t made clear at all. 

CSMs and CSPMs (middle management) make CSTLs put colleagues on plans that generate a ton of paperwork for literally zero advisor gain. These plans have continued in spite of the CSM/CSPM’s manager wanting to end plan culture, and despite CSTLs and advisors knowing they are useless.

I’ve had 4 managers in 12 months, despite being told there would be no change for a long time after I was moved to my third. My fourth has handed in her notice, two weeks in to me being part of her team.

Booking annual leave is shocking. If you don’t book it months in advance it’s down to your manager and service delivery. Most managers aren’t bothered. The annual leave system is painfully slow and breaks easily.

You often have late shifts (1pm-9pms) and early shifts (7am-3pms) scheduled right next to each other, and only get 1 full weekend in 4 off. 

Managers often aren’t process trained, so they’ll refer you to advisors instead — so, uh, what’s the point of them being managers?

New joiners increasingly act like they don’t care, which costs the business money, infuriates our customers, and means managers have to spend more time on them than on experienced colleagues who are willing to stick with the business.

Oh, and the canteen isn’t open long enough. You can only get lunch if you’re working an 8-4 or 9-5 shift, and the staff are really stuck-up.

summary: Terrible leadership ruining a great opportunity
advice:
What does all this mean for product staff? 

Product management is seen as an overhead rather than a force-multiplier. Product and channel development for actual products is non-existent. Product managers spend most of their day producing PowerPoint justifications, options papers on what the implications are of not doing (or completing) product investment. There is no recognition that this part of the bank is going down the tubes. The 2019 restructure got rid of some decent people and a couple with proper talent who I’m sure were happy to take the cheque. Others of us are now jealously waiting for our own cheque but if it’s not looking likely we might just leave anyway. Nearly as very one in this area is active on LinkedIn during (theoretical / hypothetical) lunch. Very active. 
If offered a job here I would suggest understanding which team it’s for:
If the role is in International proposition ie insight but not tangible, sellable product, then that’s well-supported but do make sure you understand the *exact* job spec as some people have left once they realised the job wasn’t what had been sold to them.
If the role is in non-product product management eg touches fin crime, Salesforce, nCino, etc then that’s also pretty well supported, again for the reasons stated. 
If the role is UK banking and deposit ‘product’ product management ie in deposits or banking solutions then I’d be cautious. Very cautious. Have you thought at all about FinTechs? Or the banks which won the RBS resolution funding? I know I am. 

Efficiencies can be driven out of this business if we invest in the infrastructure in time (ie quickly enough). Make the product systems work properly, standardise the products and make them self-serve through decent, scalable, user-friendly channels. Capital-light revenues will go up, CSAT up, staff satisfaction will go up, costs will go down. Returns go up on higher revenues AND lower costs. Will take some cash investment upfront, which is hard to secure and will mean delivering tough messages upwards (maybe just by reallocating funding from the non-product areas). If our SCCB seniors don’t bite that bullet in time, then we’re probably going down. My feeling is that the seniors haven’t got the courage to tackle their peers and others who are ‘connected’ in Madrid or to drive that message through to group.  If we do sort this out then I’ll eat my words and take this review down. But if my suspicions are correct then it might, unfortunately, already be too late. The only upside then is they’ll need us product staff to run down the business so if I can swallow my pride I’ll have work for quite a while yet.
pros:
Some terrific people trying their level best to help clients

On a returns basis, the corporate & commercial business in the UK is (a very long way) below the group’s hurdles. It is therefore undeniably in a turn-around situation.
The business was built up by lending money with the aim that, later, the ancillary revenues would grow to achieve the required returns. Much of the lending was to sectors that the big-4 abandoned post crisis eg caravan parks and care homes. These are not bad sectors per se, but they had suffered substantially in the crisis so were financially weak and there would never have been any prospect of much ancillary banking revenues. Nevertheless the previous regime of seniors allowed and encouraged it on the basis that a reasonably sized commercial bank creates a diversification play vs the 123 current account and retail mortgages (which dominate UK revenues). 

Gradually things started to change and were looking up for a couple of years. Lending started to be seen as the way to win ancillary business, rather than as an end in itself. The deposit book started to be sorted into ‘the good, the bad and the ugly’ and it looked like investment was starting to arrive.
cons:
But it turned out that the word “investment” does not mean the same to everyone. Investment in people who market things like group connectivity, sectors, alliances and general “International” insight has been given a high priority. This ‘storyline’ investment plays well in Madrid. It’s also easy to understand by the seniors, who are ex-front office RDs and structured financiers, and like anything which, on the face of it, helps the RDs to win clients. Investment in non-product infrastructure also seems to be doing ok with a £10m+ wad of cash going on nCino and other stuff related to onboarding and credit (supporting the RD community and high-capital product infrastructure). Again, the people making the decisions ‘get’ such developments. However, investment in low capital product, systems and channels such as for deposits and banking products etc has simultaneously gone off a cliff. This type of investment is just not seen as “sexy”, and the decision makers don’t want to spend money on stuff they don’t fully understand. 

Ask the UK CEO and he’ll probably say he’s invested millions into the Corporate and Commercial Bank. And he has, if you only look at the marketing and non-product types of investment. But the products’ systems are weak and the situation is getting worse. Not just on a relative basis vs the other banks, neos and FinTechs. But in absolute terms as well the systems are really creaking. This is the stuff which makes the money. Yes it’s expensive. Really eye-wateringly expensive. But no one wants to grasp this nettle. Everything else should be secondary as this is the kit which makes dough. But it’s not even of secondary importance. Not by a long stretch.

Muddying the waters are some noises from group about the EUR20bn technology fund which is for cloud-ification of the global infrastructure. But as with other developments (UK payments hub anybody?) it won’t be done in time to affect the outcomes. And UK corporate banking is (arguably?) more mature, competitive and sophisticated than corporate banking in the rest of the group. So let’s assume the key technology developments from this central programme arrive in about 4 years’ time (which might even be optimistic), and in the meantime we’ll have our product development budgets slashed further in anticipation of the central developments. But who knows whether a. the 20bn will cover everything we need to run our business, or even b. whether we will still be around to benefit from them.

They are only there to pull you up for going to the toilet or being unwell or to tell you off when you've made an error in one of the dozens of procedures we are expected to follow. 

System are an absolute joke. After spending millions on a new Investment Hub we are expected to also use an archaic banking system to process card payments. Processes change on a regular basis adding to the length of your call but you will not be given sufficient time to update your knowledge as 5 mins at the start of your shift is deemed ok for this.

Training is a joke. You will either be handed a pack of screen shots or have this read to you yet you will be expected to follow a new process to perfection even after its umpteenth change. 

Performance management is basically a popularity contest. If your pals with the right person then you will go far very quickly and get away with pretty much anything however, if you speak up or highlight any issue then prepare to get black balled. If you have the audacity to work part time then don't even bother applying for any new role or promotion. I have never seen any part timer getting promoted, ever. So you may hear about work life balance but it is a myth, it never has or will exist at Santander. 

Annual bonuses reduced this year again even though profit significantly increased.

Wage rise pretty standard however, the longer you've been there the less you get so don't expect any kind of reward for being a long term employee.

Too much time is spent fine tooth combing calls meaning ample opportunities to resolve real issues are missed. 

There are never enough advisors to handle the call volume, unfortunately no new staff can be taken on as there are so many folk off sick with stress related illness. 

Complaints process is a shambles, no support from managers who somehow always manage to be busy when you have an escalation. Do not expect to be supported in any way with this.

Back office - oh my God, where to start!- a bunch of lazy, unqualified idiots. Seriously, trained monkeys could do a better job. Totally sick of having to apologise to clients for their total incapability to read, write or function at an acceptable level. 

Santander is where common sense came to die.

Fix the staffing situation, as some branches have a number of employees while others are limited to just a few, making scheduling and pto requests a nightmare. I’ve been here for 2 years now and while I believe moving forward digitally is smart, I do not think the way the company has gone about it has been. There have been changes that have had to be undone. Changes that have been postponed, while leaving branch employees in the dark after being told that they were supposed to be giving customers a heads up on it for several months, and changes that blindsided people. We were told that the year over year growth was exceptional and yet a few months later, we watched a number of employees get laid off. While I was promoted after my first year, something like that kills the confidence in seeing opportunities to grow and move up within the company.

advice:
-Decide what is a priority to the company. There is no way a rep can do every single thing you ask, without working 50+ hours a week. If it's the numbers that are most important, take some of the needless documenting off of their plate, and let them focus on that.
-Upper management is obviously pushing dictates to the RSD's, and the "management by fear" seems to be coming straight from them. Allow the RSD's to manage their teams the way they want to. They are responsible for their numbers, so let them decide how to run the sales team. Sales teams are all unique and they don't work with a cookie-cutter approach. 
-You hired the salespeople because they're good, so give them latitude to do that.
-Micromanaging is the biggest reason people quit their jobs, is unnecessary, and makes good employees leave.
-Unfortunately, we are not "One Auto".  It is so obvious we are an "us" and "them" culture, and we all feel it.

-A lot of paperwork and edicts, but they don't give you anytime to do it, so you end up doing it during personal time in the evening and/or on weekends. Definitely a 50+ hour work week.
-Total micro-managing. They say you're the CEO of your territory, but they will tell you exactly what to do. You're a box checker.
-They will monitor how many calls you make per day, where your car is parked and for how long etc. Even though they hired you, they don't trust their reps to actually do their jobs, and they require you to account for every minute of every day. advice:
Recent turnover was more about years of frustration with a difficult work environment, and not entirely about confidence in our new management. You shook things up where that was needed, brought in some talented people from your past, and are promoting smart people who get things done, which is very refreshing.

Now we need to rebuild a team with what's left to tackle the urgent and often uninteresting work of blending with our sister and parent companies, meeting compliance requirements, and bridging years of mistrust between our technology and business organizations.

Don't ask people to put their careers on hold for the next few years. To avoid burnout, hire a few smart people to help us keep things running and open up opportunities for all of us to work on near-term innovations that will make us more productive.
pros: Self-starters may thrive here, especially with recent turnover. In the near-term your technical leadership may be rewarded if you collaborate well with technical and business teams and navigate a still-fluid organization and process.
cons:
Like other financial services providers who use dated systems, technology, and process, you'll be buried for the next several years documenting existing systems and making them comply. A lucky few will get to experiment with new technology, but most of you may have your hands full just keeping things running and meeting short-term business needs.

Lower your expectations about working on modern tech and making any major improvements, learn the business and systems, and put yourself in position to define and lead modernization in a few years.

summary: IT: from a cowboy past to a professional future
advice: Highly skilled team members aren't cheap; they're also smart enough that HR's cheerleading for the company offsets lack of base pay.  There are basic levels of compensation in the IT field such that, if they're not met, the rockstar talent necessary to a solid IT staff will go elsewhere.
pros: Santander is taking a huge leap forward with the new direction of the IT division, toward a process-driven, standards-based, carefully-managed future.  Projects are given serious forethought to manpower and capital expenditures, with the goal being that no project slips through the cracks.  This transition hasn't been without it's growing pains, but the company is taking a very serious attitude towards maintaining a professional IT organization.
cons: The transition itself, however, is the real thing. summary: Good Company with Lots of Room for Improvement
advice:
1. We have seen wayyy too many "who you know" promotions vs objective achievement causing an inadequacy of leadership and management skills amongst upper leadership.
2. Consider that each branch has different amounts and types of traffic and the goals or measurements of success reflect that much more specifically than just broken down into a few peer groups. 
3. Certain things on scorecards are completely out of the control of the respective role. Examples of such bias are:
- Sessions on teller scorecard is completely dependant on staffing makeup and branch traffic 
- Booked Credit vs Applied for Credit on banker incentive is heavily dependent on the mean and median credit worthiness of the area a particular branch serves, this effects Qualifying Accounts as well
- BOMs  referral count and sessions count should be irrelevant. Their primary role is co-managing the branch and monitoring operations while duties include training and supervising the tellers. If a branch is properly staffed, the BOM should be taking minimal transactions and helping tellers get referrals instead. 
4. Focus on hiring more people than are bilingual and properly staff said people in the appropriate communities where it is needed. We are a Spaniard bank with maybe 4 people who speak Spanish in the entire District! 
5. Too many busy branches are too small! There are literally not enough desks or computers for the appropriate amount of staff to work that have been  allotted to a branch at times. Eg. A specific branch I know is supposed to have 3 RBs and 4 Tellers a BOM and BM but has platform desks, 1 office and 3 working teller stations. What kind of nonsense is that? You can always avoid having all the RBs along with both managers available. Get some tablets and r something at least!

cons: SCUSA’s business plan is to bleed customers and to punish those who deviate from expectations.  This philosophy is applied also to employees in the call center (by far the largest aspect of the company); the company bleeds them of time, energy, and talent, hoping they’ll quit before becoming benefits-eligible.  There are no raises anywhere in the company, bonuses are frequently denied on obscure technicalities, and work schedules are intentionally burdensome.  Everyone is either miserable or angry; dozens come and go seemingly weekly, company-wide.  SCUSA exploits an IT department populated by immigrants utterly chained to their employer; few are broadly knowledgeable about technologically or even basic business practices (or even intermediate English), while most are essentially captive labor.  There is also a tendency to fire IT workgroups after pet projects are completed or cancelled, meaning IT employment is only reliable in three-week increments-- happened to me after two years.

There is always enough work to go around, you will never be bored at Santander! Like any bank, we are also heavy on policy, procedure, compliance, but have not found a way to make this part of the job painless.

pros: Santander has sincerely made the commitment to staying in the US, and is looking to grow after turning-around a dysfunctional entity in the US (fmr Sovereign Bank).  Conservative staffing policy will prevent layoffs unless the US has a severe economic relapse.
cons:
Extremely conservative philosophy in regards to expenses unfortunately extends to employee compensation.  You might say the turnaround from being insolvent to several quarters of growth was made "on the employees backs".  Base compensation was frozen across-the-board for several years while benefits were substantially cut, to the point that they had to give some benefits back over the past couple of years, or there would have been a massive employee exodus.

Their staffing model has been to heavily invest in young (read: cheap) talent through their their Santander Universities outreach initiative, and heavily in technology standardizing business processes.  This way, when an employee leaves, they could just plug-in another fresh graduate.

Anyone looking to rise through Santander US corporate ranks could expect to do so only in Boston.

summary: European bank values leisure, but doesn’t value raises.
advice:
The Company is literally pouring money into unnecessary job functions and even whole departments! So many jobs and processes can be EASILY automated to save you thousands upon thousands of dollars in employee costs. Spend a little extra on modernizing your systems today, and it is guaranteed to pay for itself. You will save money on hiring, training, and paying employees (not to mention on benefits, unemployment, etc).

Two departments (Compliance and HR)  should get a complete overhaul. Compliance seems to have whole teams dedicated to just a few regulations (if that). That is absurd! How does that make an ounce of sense? Frankly, most of them do irrelevant reviews and pester you for weeks like it’s normal. Come to find out, they’re annoying you over past data! Not just months past, but sometimes it’s been years! They don’t offer any business insight by being a year behind. I’d automate compliance in a heartbeat.

Now, HR, can’t be as easily automated as Compliance but boy they deserve to be. HR is so incompetent it actually poses a serious business risk. Compliance where you at? From a legal standpoint or any standpoint really, they are a liability by being as incapable as they are right now. Their lack of  necessary skills has completely exploited the system for what it is. Truth is, it is very easy to manipulate and take advantage of the system in place (sad how many people do this). These people are then reinforced to further exploit the system because they can! HR’s lack of record keeping, nonexistent analytical insights, and just overall incompetence on all fronts will bring the downfall of this company. I would cut the entire HR department and start over.
pros:
Ok, so never getting a raise sucks- but if you can look past pay,  they offer great benefits and the atmosphere is bearable. People are GENERALLY nice. This company  definitely has MANY perks:

•  22-28 days PTO (option to buy even more!)
• Medical, Dental, Vision
• Free STD, LTD, and AD&D insurance
• Counseling and Legal Assistance
• 401K (3-5% match)
• Tuition Reimbursement
• Computer Purchase Program
• Discounts and Travel Deals (not that great)

The work is either stressful or a  complete breeze. Corporate and upper management want to stress meeting deadlines - and for good reason. The deadlines are attainable. Could I finish a quarterly review 2 weeks early? Probably. Will I? Not a chance.

Leisure is valued here.
cons:
Ok, so here’s the big secret at Santander - overall, the work is really not overwhelming. But, people here are accustomed to the comfortable pace - so, when management tries tightening deadlines, they get resistance. It’s almost laughable. It really hinders any realistic growth for this company.

If you get a raise or bonus at all, it will be a measly 2% (if that). People who work less hard, get less pay - seems to be everybody’s trade off here. Oh, and the technical problems are infinite. Outdated systems would be a blessing - we use fossils.

Nobody gets fired here, but I’ve seen a few incidents recently where managers and HR were using some underhanded methods to get an employee fired. Witnessing this definitely reinforced my decision to leave.
