cons: Organizations & infrastructure changes a lot. Move from one team to another. There is an inconsistency between teams in how people are managed. The company still lags in the US in technology which can add extra time to many daily tasks and projects. Constant changes to policy

summary: Not a stable company at all.
advice: Stop constantly laying people off. You are stalling any progress that is being achieved and you are losing trust of employees.
pros: I had a good team.
cons: I spend less than 3 years at the company and they changed our manager 4 times in that short time period. Impossible to achieve any goals because your teammates and managers are constantly getting laid off. The worst part is that smart, hard-working people are the ones that are being cut. Higher mgmt only looks at the salaries, not the work quality. Employees are always on a lookout, waiting to be laid off. Communication between departments is terrible. Wasting time holding meeting after meetings but almost never actually achieving anything. There is lots of irresponsibility and serious lack of accountability.

summary: New SPF culture (Simple Personal and Fair)
advice: Remove old school hierarchical managers. Bring in new international managers with multicultural experience, implement 360 performance review. Introduce Grievance and Disciplinary independent department not reporting to HR. Cero tolerance to bullying, mobbing and harassing attitudes. Coach HR managers to explain their responsibility as guardians of the "culture change" and their required position of neutrality in conflicts.
pros: Great culture change for the bank, but many hurdles and internal management resistance / barriers to make it happen
cons: Still old style managers in place with old rigid and not innovative culture / attitudes: extreme hierarchical views and attitudes, with cero acceptance to challenge, and with lack of respectful manners. There is no formal grievance processes in place to denounce unacceptable managerial behaviors. HR old school department takes positions on Management side leaving employees helpless and at their own stake.

advice: Be honest about your bonus policy and find a way to meet deadlines without overworking employees.
pros: The annual salary was decent.  The company said they would give you a big bonus.   The company definitely worked you hard.  I worked in the Dallas office
cons: The understood concept with management was meet your deadline at all costs.  Not much work life balance at all.  There was 75%+ turnover in the accounting department in the year while I was there.  Definitely a stressful environment.  They say they will give you a big bonus, but they don't really give much of a bonus to new employees.  You have to make it through a whole calendar year first.  They tend to hire from outside for managers as well.

advice: Please spend money on your technology and remove these micromanaging processes you have tracking your every move on high level bankers.  But on the flipside, your process is the reason I am leaving banking for bigger things and for that I thank you.
pros: Great opportunities to grow and learn feom colleagues.
cons: A very high level of micromanagement for a high level position.  Every client requires a submission of conversation details to manager, mid and post session review; doesn’t matter if client is in a rush.  For the first time in 14 years, I want to proactively leave banking.  Also technology is very antiquated that can cause simple processes like opening accounts to take 1.5 hours even for an experienced banker.  There is paper filing for everything on top of that and not flexibility on those processes.

summary: Not a place you want to work at
pros: Unfortunately, I had a very miserable experience at Santander in New York. They are quite effective recruiters, but once you are in, you realize you have been lied to and most of the 'facts' you were told are simply untrue. A very frustrating place to work at, with very hierarchical management that simply won't listen (many of them Spanish expats who are here for a couple of years and then leave), and a very "old school" approach to everything. Very resistant to any type of change, technology or suggestion for improvement.
cons: Salaries (base) are low. But they promise very high bonuses that unfortunately are never achieved even if one (as in my case) exceeds sales and revenue goals by 50%! Again, a culture of lies and excuses. Extremely old fashioned place where managers will literally yell and scream at every little chance they get. I was truly miserable at this place.

advice: Please invest in your people and your brand. Give your employees the time, tools and motivation to be successful.
pros: Decent benefits, some areas of growth depending on your skills (real & political)
cons: Not a good work-life balance. Long hours expected for branch staff. Compensation is average and quarterly incentive amount and structure is not motivating. Limited opportunities here in New York since most non-Retail positions are located in PA and MA. There has been constant turn over for both Branch staff, Middle and Senior Management which has made it difficult for the brand to maintain a constant unified vision and path to success. There needs to be serious investment into technology and staffing for the bank to improve, however Executive Management has made it clear that such investments are not feasible.

pros: Good Pay and Benefits, the program is very good as well for any qualified clients.  Management rating depends not eh branch as you are working for a branch manager and a District Executive which could be a crap shoot.
cons: A lot of employees do not understand the program or how it works.  The investment side of the bank is in complete chaos.   Financial Consultants leave after a year or so.  Investments are a major part of your business and clients are loath to trust you with their investments because of high turnover at FC position and at branch.

advice: Change the bonus system.  Value your employees.
pros: I'm stay here in hope that policies will change.  Business outlook is good.
cons: Bonuses are mostly based on the luck of the draw.  Employees with the least charged off accounts are eligible for the largest  bonus. Our files are shuffled monthly.  .In my department only two employees were in the top 25% for 3 or more months in the last six months.  There are approximately 110 employees in this department,  The top 50% may receive a bonus.  They use "call miner"  a phone system which detects any type of violation.  One miscue and you lose your bonus for up to 3 months and if you don't get a good "book" you are eventually  terminated.

summary: Worst Company I've ever worked for.
advice: Clean out the multiple layers of middle management and pay and treat branch level employees who are the face of the brand with the customers better.
pros: The potential to be on the ground floor of a large international bank as it expands into the US market.
cons: Too many layers of ineffective middle management, aggressive sales driven culture that does not have the customers best interest in mind. Constantly changing bonus structure to make it less attainable. Employees are constantly lied to and not given the courtesy of a reply or even acknowledgement when grievances aired. A former co-worker applied for multiple open positions that he was qualified for and was left not knowing the status of his application despite his inquires, all because he wasn't in tight with management he stood no chance of ever advancing but instead of telling him one way or the other they just said nothing until he finally wised up to their game and found a much better paying jog elsewhere.

advice: Hire management without substance abuse issues as it does effected their job performance. Be available to employees as it is them who make the company and HR needs to review the mgmt members more often as they are not saints!
pros: The NRH location was close and the job wasn't difficult. The pay was decent and bonuses were paid monthly.
cons: The department is ran by an absentee mgr that's nice but hardly available. The other 2 mgrs are rude hard to deal with have blatant favorites are moody fickle dishonest disorganized and way to involved in their own personal issues to be effective supervisors. When I started all the long term ppl were transferring to other depts and said this was just a foot in the door position. There are no raises and if you brought up issues you were targeted as a trouble maker written up for bogus reasons until they can fire you. I've heard positive things about every other dept so try ANYTHING BUT ROADLOANS!

summary: A few great perks, but no moral & limited growth
advice: All in all, some managers get it right & others simply do not care. Develop your PB's & implement Wealth Management like so many of our counterparts. Santander loves the Stack Ranking so I encourage you to do so while coaching those with the propensity to be successful. If those directly under you consistently under perform, its a reflection of your leadership & the talent you keep. Cut the weak links in the chain & remove those who consistently show they are not here to make Santander the #1 global bank. Manage the right talent for the growth we wish to have. World wide integration would be practical & is expected. Continue to do anonymous survey's & we will tell you our opinion, since you clearly don't read these reviews.
pros:
As a Premier Banker, the incentive plan is by far one of the best I've had. I love that Santander allows an open forum from its employees to make Real Changes, every month! The recommendations for improvement are implemented within 1 year on average, but there is IMPROVEMENT! I also love that Santander rewards hard. You can expect high quarterly bonuses & annual merit raises up to 5%. 
The support team, Santander Assist, is great in helping employees with troubleshooting on the spot. Moreover, the Operations Managers are one of the few departments that have common sense. Not sure how this helps, but its nice to receive advisement from people who can articulate passed giving out a roll of quarters. Also, we recently implemented an escalation process called CARE that resolves clients service request quickly & efficiently. Again, this is already established in most banks, however a major leap for Santander. The salary is competitive if you're job grade 8+. Otherwise, you can not afford the products & services you sell to everyone else.
cons:
I have worked for Santander for 4 yrs now. I previously worked for PNC where moral, ethics, & career growth were structured. Those are three major things missing from Santander and they are well aware of it. We do team building events once a quarter but this hardly improves moral. Sadly, like most banks, Santander hires high school grads with little to no college or financial experience & expects them to make life changing recommendations for consumer's assets. Hell, most employees think the N.A. stands for North America. Most branch team members are on their phones all day texting instead of giving their best to the client experience. Client experience is measured, however not managed as closely as most retail banks.
Its absurd to work with upper and direct management with no educational background. The blind leading the blind as they say. Additionally, managers who over delegate BKA complacency syndrome get upset when their employees receive a bonus, however they don't for lack of overall branch productivity. If you do your part, then you'd also reap in the harvest.
There needs to be career-pathing for Premier Bankers. The most we can hope for is Select Banker & those positions are few & far between. 
Lastly, our systems constantly crash & there are network-wide emails that script how to properly apologize for the "crisis-of-the-day." Santander Consumer USA, who does the financing through dealerships are disrespectful & rude. It'd be nice to see these loans on our system so we can avoid calling SCUSA.

advice: It should be wise for upper management to look and evaluate what district executives are doing at times. I have already witnessed four valuable top performers teammates leaving Santander because of bad treatment and non qualified promotions.
pros: Very well known bank around the world. Great opportunities if you play the politics. Pay is good.
cons: Not the best life/work balance. Although I was one of the top performers and promised a promotion, new upper management felt that I had to wait. Instead they gave the job to somebody else. Cliques and politics are the right words for it.

advice: Provide a payplan that is fair and gives the employee the ability to be aggressive and work it. Don't change it multiple times a year because that takes the "sales" initiative out of it and shows you don't know what you are doing.  People throw their hands up and say I'll do just enough to get by and make what they give me. Stop micromanaging! Give your ASM/RSM a number to hit and let them hit it any way they can. If they don't, don't pay them. It's bad enough when we don't hit our numbers and don't get paid.....it's worse having to deal with the BS micromanagement throughout the process and afterwards. Don't you think I like money? Of course I do, that is motivation enough. If you feel your employee needs micromanagement, then you didn't do a good job hiring for an outside account management position in the first place. Get some outside ideas in the place. All of management has been promoted from within. They all think the same and manage the similarly. It's ok to hire an RSM or Director from outside of the institution.
pros: Flexibility in work schedule, compensation is above average. You are provided the ability to work you day as you see fit (to a point).
cons: As soon as they went public, it's been down hill for employees. The have started to squeeze the payplan and control every dime. When I started you could make over $115k, now you're luck to make $93k. You are really only given the chance to control your pay by 5%. You get laughed out of dealerships because the program is so bad (but you do get paid decently for it).  With the lending program as it is, all you do is beg for applications. It is really brainless work. It's a perfect job if you don't mind micromanagement and don't want to continually progress professionally. It is just a very simple minded job.Most of low level management has only worked here so their management skills are more micromanagement than applying interpersonal skills. They do not seem to have experience managing to the individual person.

summary: Good people, good balance, but terrible processes and compensation.
advice: Want to stop constantly backfilling key positions? Be more proactive at compensation. Stop being so cheap, especially when the business is clearly having some of its best results. The turnover-over is starting to get demoralizing, and making me question if I am hurting my future earnings potential for unrewarded loyalty.
pros: They do well hiring good personalities, and it's an enjoyable work life balance.
cons: Your pay goes up when you climb the ladder, or use the company as stepping stone. They can't retain any non-director level talent because their competitors simply have better base pay.

summary: IF YOU DESIRE TO KNOW HOW THE HELL IS, COME TO SANTANDER BANK
advice:
Show more respect to the employees.
Allow employees to reach a balance between work and family
The employees are people no machines
Sometimes a employee has better ideas than a boss, so they should listen to the employees
pros:
Desperation
Cheap loans
Masochism
To be keen on seeing a rustic managing an international bank
cons:
Low salaries
Bad work environment
Too much stress
Is like a sect (sectarian behaviour)
Very long work periods
They must know where you are in any moment (exhaustive control, no trust)
The company is the prior thing and sometimes employees do illegal duties (recommend to buy shares to clients that Santander wants to get rid off; no accept recomendations of Bank of Spain nor Central European Bank, lie to clients to contract their services despite of high risks, ...)

advice: Keep up the good work and continue to boast your employees spirits with great rewards. You are all doing a phenomenal job.
pros: This is a great company to work for that allows you to have a balanced work/home life. The benefits of working for this company are overwhelmingly awesome and they truly care about their employees best interest and their families. Competive salary ranges, safe fun working environment, an HR department that is extremely helpful, and overall just a great place to work.
cons: I cannot say that I have any cons with my current position or the company overall.

pros: Banco Santander is a leading retail and commercial bank, based in Spain, with a meaningful market share in 10 core countries in Europe and the Americas. Santander is the largest bank in the euro zone by market capitalization and among the top 12 banks on a global basis. Founded in 1857, Santander had EUR 1.43 trillion in managed funds, 12,950 branches and 185,400 employees at the close of 2014. In 2014 Santander made an attributable profit of EUR 5,816 million, 39% more than the previous year.
cons: Santander is a amazing company, but with no place to unefficient people

advice:
Clearly state a career path from the beginning, with goals and milestones for each candidate
Promote more mobility initiatives among the offices in the world
pros:
- Good exposition to M&A and Project Finance teams from around the Globe
- Access to international clients
- Good coordination with other internal teams for support (treasury, loans)
- Important brand in IB in Latin America and Iberia
cons:
- Career path, although follows IB standard (Analyst/Associate/VP/ED/MD), is not laid out clearly. There's no "timing" for the advancements to happen
- Revenue sharing among offices in cross-border deals does not help the build a collaborative spirit

summary: Perhaps the DUMBEST people I have ever met. This is why Elizabeth Warren HATES banks!
advice: Ana Botin should sell the US bank ASAP.
pros: NONE! Oh wait...they just got rid of the worst, most pompous executive. The old saying "what goes around, comes around" rings true thankfully!
cons: Some of the dumbest people I have worked with in my career that has spanned 20 plus years in Financial Services. Everything is broken - Technology, processes, people. How about start with the golden rule - treat others as you would like to be treated.  I knew there was a reason why I never opened a bank account here when I joined. I never trusted the company - and once you see behind the curtain....you might be ill.

advice: Improve the way harassment complaints from employees are handled. Would have saved me from contacting an attorney!
pros: As a branch manager while employed at Santander, I met a lot of good coworkers. Other than that, I can’t think of any other pros.
cons: The culture of the bank was absolutely horrendous. The best branch managers I knew, along with the best mortgage officers and financial consultants, all left the bank within the last year or two. Sales practices were becoming unethical, and any problems you may have with District Executives are ignored when reported to HR. I have also worked for Citizens Bank and Bank of America, and I would recommend working for one of those banks, or perhaps a smaller institution. BEWARE OF SANTANDER!

summary: the worst company I have ever worked for, and a loser among banks for a reason obvious to employees
advice: -honestly, you need to rethink the entire structure of the company. I'd clean out all of the upper management and hire people who actually work in the branch. too often you will talk to upper management and they will have no idea what you are talking about. management also abuses other management with weak personalities to prove that their strategies work.
pros:
-extreme mobility (due to frustrating culture, turnover, and general incompetence)
-good way to break into industry
cons:
-no lunch breaks
-horribly understaffed with management too lazy to do work themselves
-no control of your schedule, no days off
-unpaid overtime
-so much management and too few actual workers
-micromanagement of every aspect of your day
-computer system crashes every day
-embarassing and impossible most times to actually support customers
-this company breaks labor laws consistently and nothing is done about it. they would rather sit around and talk about statistically invalid customer service scores, low outbound call volume which angers and confuses most customers, and yell at tellers/bankers for not getting more referrals and revenue.
-they have a toxic production culture, where you spend so much time micromanaging producting and customer service that you don't get time to do any of it.
-honestly I am going to file a lawsuit against this company before I leave.

summary: Culture change from a great place to work to a crappy sweat shop environment  after 7 1/2 years
advice:
Replace the CIO who not only is mindful of the bottom line, but what drives people to want to be successful in the company
Give IT technologist a career pathway
Stop talking at people and listen to what they are saying.  They are you most important resource.
pros: Great benefits such as vacation time, medical, etc
cons:
Poor IT leadership
Became too expensive to work downtown and the company provided no incentive
Lack of direction
Too much cronyism
Became more of a sweatshop environment with no work\life
Allowed outside unqualified individuals to dictate solutions not in their area
Panic management and disorganization due to very poor planning and failure to listen to knowledgeable individuals
Fail to retain qualified people and when they left, slow to no movement to replace them
Outdated technology (back end)  which also hindered bringing new IT Technologist since it is a career killer to work with out dated technology and not plans to move forward, even though new technology was desperately needed.
Exit interview produced no results for those employees who were left

summary: Just short of five, but here is why
advice: Personally, I am very at Santander. I know that there are many things that are out of the management's control and that is ok. Just keep on doing what you are doing, and above all, keep on letting the employees know what is going on. We feel appreciated and more dedicated if people know what is going on.
pros:
- Benefits. The 401k is a 5% match after just one month of service! This is fully vested as well!
The vacation time is very generous, can carry over 5 days. Most colleagues start with 3 weeks of vacation.
- Incentive is very generous compared to every other bank in the area.
- The middle management is fairly solid. Since this is a smaller bank, they want to see you succeed. 
- Company is very transparent with their plans. It makes it easier to follow the vision of upper management.
cons:
- Technology. Hardware is very outdated, and it is hard to multitask.
- Some bankers will find it very hard to earn a solid payout.
- Internal transfers are hard.
- The base pay could be a little better

advice: Stop faking HR and teach your management how to actively and effectively manage employees.  Spend some $ on office improvements and overall technology.  Upgrade the infrastructure.  Set delivery expectations that are realistic and allow IT to be a part of the scheduling process up front.
pros: Lots of smart individual contributors at the employee level.  There were some "fun" events every quarter.
cons:
Management has no problem setting unrealistic deadlines for IT delivery and then expecting night and weekend work in order to meet the deadline.  Bonus levels are dictated based on how much you "brown nose" and/or how well your manager likes you.   Pay rate is below market.  Office location and setup is terrible and done on the cheap - packed like sardines in a tin can.  Micro management runs rampant.  Directors like to play games and threaten "to bring in HR" for any little issue or perceived problem.  Border line racism for non-Indian employees.  VP's simply look the other way if things go bad.  Managers still have to "approve" your vacation days.  Gossip and infighting about little things are common.  

Why people tolerate this environment is beyond me.  This is not a healthy employee environment.

summary: Work here at your own risk!
advice: Clean house and stop trying to be like every other big bank out there. Be innovative and disruptive, and be smart about it (not like extra20).
pros: It’s a job. They pay a decent salary and you get a lot of vacation days. If you want, you can easily get by without doing much real work - I’ve seen people that have been employed at Santander for years that haven’t produced anything.
cons:
If you like to go to work and feel a sense of accomplishment, this is not the place for you. Things move very slowly, if at all, and you very rarely have any high-level insight into what you’re working on. I’ve worked at much larger companies that had much more transparency.

To put it bluntly, the upper management is horrible. It’s a very political environment, filled with people who have mostly failed at larger, more successful banks. It’s a recipe for disaster - bring in a bunch of “industry experts” that were not successful at BofA, Chase, Citi, etc. and put them in management positions. There is no clear-cut strategy to win.

If this sounds bad to you, then do yourself a favor, and do not take a job here, unless you really have no other choice.

advice: To the Management above the Vice Presidents. You have seen the IT GRC turnover rate setting records. Surely you have  heard other VPs and Directors complaining about the management in IT GRC. You should interview those VPs, directors and even IT GRC staff and make the necessary changes before IT GRC continues to damage Santanders reputation. Because of so many leaving and sharing their stories thereafter, IT GRCs reputation is external to Santander at this point.
pros: Professional development was strongly discouraged. It's not Santander it's IT GRC. Training literature from professional organizations or external training could not be shared. Yes you read that correctly. Or the manager with many certifications would slap you on the wrist. That happened twice. That alone solidified my decision to leave. Extreme unprofessionalism. It was hard to focus on work concerned about who from management would backstab next. Initially you never knew where the fables were coming from, but ultimately you didnt care. You just wanted out. Middle and top management supported the unprofessionalism and oiled it's wheels. It was so tiring it took twice as much effort just to search for another job. The door out of IT GRC was like a fan at it's highest setting.
cons: Ridiculously poor management. Extremely high Turnover. Very unprofessional.

advice: Being in a leadership role is a title, being able to actually lead and make people want to follow is what is important. Anna is the only only manager at the location that genuinely wants better for the employees, the other managers have proven over and over again they are just there for a paycheck.
pros: Building is nice, I guess.
cons:
-You get 10 minutes a week of personal time/bathroom time, 2 minutes a day. I have never felt more like a child in my life. MAKE SURE TO BRING A DIAPER.
-Preach advancement but hire from the outside rather then promote within. 
-Almost every position besides becoming a manger is "lateral" meaning you will not get a raise but they expect more work out of you. Also they will force you to these departments if you are consistently hitting bonus so they don't have to pay you. 
-Highest raise they give annually is .4% (which is around .50 cents) only to top performers (no one knows the criteria to being considered a top performer)
-HR has a "closed door policy"... if something is bothering you make sure to schedule and appt. through email and hopefully they email you back a few days later. Kind of defeats the purpose of HR.

pros:
- Located in one of the nicest office buildings in downtown
- Flexible schedule and culture
- Likely you will experience little to no supervision
- Good work/life balance
- Everyone pretends they care
cons:
- You may work hard and not advance very far only to see others as exceptions to this rule. I assure you those folks are tied to a E/C/VP/SVP (daughter, friends kid, college buddy, former colleague).
- The company tells employees to strive for "customer" excellence which is ironic to their whole business model. It is not a company goal at the end of the day.
-  Those who leave are never backfilled. You are expected to pick up the slack. 
-  No direction. You may find the boys club at the YMCA playing basketball.
-  Leadership is a tight knit network of people who have been buddies for a long time. They only hire people they know. This is how they retain their six figure salaries doing little to no work.

advice: Take care of your employees. Win their hearts and minds. It's not going to happen by hooking up your friends with jobs. There is no hope past the branch beyond a lateral move.
pros: Competitive products and some talented colleagues. Good footprint. Overall everyone is pretty nice, they just feel the pressure rolling down hill.
cons: The career patting is all for show. The attrition is off of the charts for a reason. People can't see a future and the incentive plan is a profit and loss system directly from Citizens Bank along with the staff who created it. That relates back to career. All senior positions are from friends of friends from other banks (Citizens, JP Morgan, Bank of America) the branches and business bankers are the face of the bank, literally the most talented people are sprinting to the doors! Of course they will fill the positions with new people that will have to go through training and build a pipeline so there will be a lot of less production in the year over year revenue.

advice: Communicate more, provide training and set clear attainable expectations. Demonstrate career possibilities and vet who you hire more thoughtfully for the existing set of challenges. Don't tolerate leaders who are sacrificing others to cover their inadequacies.
pros: Some very nice, kind people, some very capable people. International culture. There are good areas of the bank and a chance to grow the corp. side but retail mentality is pervasive. If you can discern where the influencers are, you can do well.  Understanding Spanish language and culture can be advantageous.
cons: No real sense of direction or consistency most of the time. New hires are not well supported in many areas, no training, just thrown in the mix and have to figure it out. If you are a quick study, you can do well. Cultural issues between Spanish global bank leadership and old Sovereign Bank folk are distinct. Add a layer of JP Morgan (not all the cream of the crop) and it can get messy trying to navigate. There is epic turnover in some areas.

advice: Random suggestion. Try installing rotating art in the halls. This can give the cube farm staff a chance to discover new cultures, perspectives, and therefore ideas.
pros: Very good pay plus bonus, and benefits. Work from home flexibility is helpful considering Boston traffic. Campus offices have gyms. Casual dress (if you think that is a Pro).  Did I mention very good pay?
cons: This is where the trade off is from the Pros. No frills. No offices and very few/ not enough conference rooms. Just long tables with monitors to plug in your computer. Is this normal? I had an office with a door and a window at my old job. One of the campus offices is old and has mice. IT infrastructure is quite bad. Frequent outages. 10 million passwords for all your applications.

summary: From retail to banking - WOW what a difference!
advice: Don’t stop evolving to be better - it’s what makes this company different!
pros:
-Training is very well thought out, very structured, very supportive. Training never stops, and you never stop learning!
-Team is super supportive. From having a Peer Mentor, to the district team being available at all times, it’s a supportive environment.
-You dictate how your training goes - be the boss of your training progress!
-Company is customer focused - every meeting or conference call is ALWAYS about the customer being first - love that culture.
cons:
-Some training sessions are long and pack a ton of info.
-If you like constant structure, it isn’t dictated at all times. It’s not necessarily a negative, but if you want constant structure and being told what to do, it’s not going to be constant.

advice: Invest in upgrading your servicing portals to improve customer service, instead off sending every little thing to back office to process. Is also very time consuming to work with a customer in front of you with their slow and outdated software.
pros: Good place to start your career in the banking industry.
cons: Their system to provide service is really old. Now they trying to go universal, so they won't have to  pay additional employees and the only results are going to be worst customer service, because now every team member is only looking for sales and if somebody comes with an issue nobody wants to take care of it.(all they had to do was hire an extra part time teller in every branch). Please wake-up this branches are not in store branches like citizens.

advice: Identify who and what you want to be as a company and move in that direction with purpose. Management, you know what's wrong so fix it by tackling the low hanging fruit and take care of the issues related to personnel. Provide meaningful communication to the masses. Practice consistency and responsiveness. Management needs to execute.
pros:
Competitive pay at or above industry
Great work experience for building skills
Competitive health benefits at or above industry
Prominent downtown Dallas Location
Good talent pool and nice people to work with
cons:
No company culture, brand, or identity to speak of
Very weak mid-level and senior leadership
Inconsistent and non-defined career paths
Constant regulatory and legal troubles
Weak vacation policy below industry
Dated, manual methodologies, processes, and business practices
Lack of top down communication
Slow and/or non-responsive reaction to feedback from employees
Lack of execution on numerous initiatives

advice: Banking is continually stressful and competitive. Without a supportive staff and good management, it is a very tough working atmosphere. The rules change continually, there is no room for error, there is nepotism, backstabbing in a cutthroat culture.
pros: Definitely a great place to learn about the basic rules and regulations of the banking industry. Very diverse employees of all backgrounds, cultures, and religions.
cons: Management changes its mind every... wait it doesn't make up its mind, no decisions are ever made, and if they are, they're optional anyway. Surprise! Constant unfilled attrition, employees stay on rarely more than a year. Most people could care less. Technological dinosaur using cheap, unsupported, and not understood "proprietary" systems from Spain. Clowns. Think clowns stuffed in a small car except it's so sad, it's never funny. Incompetence run amuck. Dimwitted, clueless management with no education or fraud experience. And attrition rate is off the charts! Good people being quietly terminated, or quitting all the time!

summary: Clique Central: If you are a puppet, you will do well here.

summary: Do not waste your time with Santander
advice: Work to make actual change instead of putting off the impression the bank is something that it is not. The Respect Campaign is not reflective of how associates or clients feel. The constant turnover is not a positive.

cons:

advice: Make big changes or this bank will go under.  Either that or ALL of your employees will be incompetent, not just some.  Highly talented professionals realize this and leave quickly.

summary: Ask alot of questions when interviewing.

No I was not fired I quit as did the other three people before me.  If I knew that the work environment was as it was no way would I have taken that job. About the trainee position: your first months will be like an evaluation period until the internship gets approved by a public service (IEFP), so you will be highly underpaid, and work like everybody else. Hourly salary is decent
cons: They are pretty strict about clock in/out times. Job gets very boring when not talking to live customers and just leaving messages. Most customers are sub prime loans and not very educated when it comes to understanding simple interest or car loans.

advice:

Most of the managers had never supervised or had any management experience managing people. pros: They will hire anyone even the neighborhood drug dealer because they don't drug test.

cons: Micromanagement, no work from home (though I do not understand the reason behind it as the type of work we did was easily manageable from home and more over it was more cost effective for the company.)To get your PTO accepted you need to have luck. advice:
It's probably not surprising that since the corporate re-alignment in April, that Glassdoor may be blowing up with some negative criticism.  My intent with this review is to highlight the same exact issues I've been talking to leadership for years -- yet nothing seems to change.  Don Goin's entrance was heralded as the single most catalytic event to transform IT.  So, I am not surprised a corporate re-alignment occurred.  600+ IT people in a company this size is, without argument, ridiculous.

My advice to Jason Kulas and Don Goin are:

- Re-evaluate IT leadership's ability to execute.  Operations and Project Management are key weak areas.  Have been weak areas for years and many are disheartened and fearful to speak up due to labeling and punitive reprocutions.  Yes, this exists under your leadership.  Ferit it out with more 'Donuts with Don'.

- Re-evaluate the leadership over Enterprise Architecture and ask what business value it provides today.  Arguably the single most profitable asset for SC, it's constantly under attack from leaders across IT:  Information Security, Risk, GRC, Business Intelligence, Application Development, on and on.  What is business enabling?  What are our integration opportunities?  Fix workplace integration first, with a great communications and messaging platform.

- Embrace something.  DevOps, ITILv3, SAFe.  Let's get all in.  Train critical people.  Re-establish culture.  Manage out the poor performers.  Manage in the people who get it.  Promote them up.  Culture, Automation, Measure, and Sharing.  80% is not good enough for high performing companies, any longer and, as calibration last year proved, you have some major issues to fix to get this actually working properly.

- Values mean something.  First year at SC, I was told, we have no values.  Now, we have values, but are we living by them?  Simple and Fair should be embraced at all levels of the architecture.  Yet, so many people in IT would categorize their environments as not simple and unfair.  Do not depend on your leaders to fix it themselves.  They are comfortable in their fiefdom and attack progress or change.  Culture is tantamount to success for high performing organizations.  Fix this first.
pros:
- "SC" has many great teams, with people who genuinely want to do great work for the organization.  I've worked with many awesome people and felt these people get it.

- You will be exposed to many things outside your career field, giving you many opportunities to grow and learn.  Everything from audits and controls to documentation and projects.

- Some leaders are great and will mentor you.  Find them and hold onto them.
cons:
- Most complex environment in 20+ years.  Overly and unabashedly complex making simple tasks take days, if not weeks.    Suggestions often get ignored or your told to "keep quiet and just do what I say."  Why hire people and not listen to their expertise and advice?  IT's complexity caused by overly reactive and poor Infomration Security leadership and poor governance and oversight by Risk and GRC, astromically increasing complexity.

- Poor IT middle management.  MBA's flaunt their credentials and are often problematic getting anything done.  One leader told me, "You need to stop reading books.  Just listen to me and you'll be fine."  Trying to change culture to improve processes usually result in negative feedback and "interpersonal savvy difficulties."  Consensus amongst peer managers that leadership is a major problem under CIO, Don Goin.  Many hope Don cleans house.

- Poor strategic outlook.  Unable to measure.  Everything last minute.  Heavy criticisms on performance yet, no strategic plan, no understanding what goals we are trying to hit, no consistent KPI, yet lots of TPS reports and questionably valueable last minute work.  These poor leaders often heard commenting, "we just don't have the right people".  Don's efforts to change usually results in amazing pressure on Directors or below to whip up some metrics.  Don's directs rarely involved or engaged other than levying criticism.

- Cherry picks ideas, but embraces none.  ITIL, DevOps, SAFe, all are not fully embraced and many gray areas exist.  Mass confusion on what to do, when to do it, and who owns it.  ServiceNow gets focus for a little while, then SharePoint, then WordPress.  Policies, procedures, metrics, all ambigiously implemented and poorly maintained.  Attempts to fix are often quashed.

- Interpersonal savvy is the core trait valued over all others.  Do not professionally disagree with leaders or argue the merits of ideas over standard quo.  These people are labeled, discredited, disrespected, and managed outward.  Yet, those same folks are often the catalysts for change and people focused.  Heavy amounts of sucking up to leaders through personal compliments go further father than actually getting things done on time.  High performers seen letting go because they, "didn't suck up to leaders, enough."  Wow.

summary: Stable company, poised for success, but improvement is needed
advice: Current market conditions are providing a perfect opportunity for Drive to make a statement in the industry and carve out a much larger market share.  However, customer service and fees are hurting our ability to take advantage of our strength and current market conditions.  Dealers are turning away from Drive and pursuing competitors for these reasons.  If the program cannot be changed due to ROI minimums, then at the very least customer service should be made a priority. The attitude of employees (funding and credit) towards dealers has to be addressed.  The success of future programs (ie B paper program) and Drive as a whole is contingent upon these improvements.
pros: Despite the current economy and sluggish market segment (subprime auto loans), the company has shown stability during these turbulent times and adaptability to changes in environment.  While other, larger competitors have cut loan originations by 50-80% in the last year, Drive Financial has maintained a fairly stable level of loan originations.  Mid-level management is supportive and understanding of front line employees as they were once front line workers themselves.  There is a commraderie (sp?) among the front line employees, especially in the sales department.  While career advancement is somewhat limited by virtue of being a smaller company, employees are given the opportunity to standout.  Employees that do perform are recognized.  The company is poised for success when the economy turns around because of lack of competitors in the market place and backing of the parent company (Europe's largest by market cap) Santander.
cons: Uncertainty in the market place has led to the conserative decisions and programs.  These decisions make reaching commission goals difficult and therefore pay has suffered.  Sales representatives that survived two rounds of layoffs have had pay cut by 20-30% in the last year.  Unfortunately, customer service is not made a priority by leadership and the sentiment is transfered down to non-sales employees.  Customers are often turned off by the lack of customer service provided by the company as a whole.  Those not comfortable with change would not do well at this company as change is a constant.  Those able to 'roll with the punches' will do fine.

This bank will probably not be around in the near future.

summary: Great opportunities for those who want a career in banking and sales
advice: Stop setting impossible sales targets and low quarterly payouts for tellers
pros: I work with some great people that actually make working here bearable. You get holidays off and there are good benefits like medical, dental, PTO etc. You will learn a lot about banking and finance for an entry level position. A great starting position especially if you plan on moving up to a personal banker or branch manager and making this your career.
cons: Heavy on sales goals. But then again, what bank isn't right? I will literally receive harassing e-mails from the district executive every day about checking account goals or credit card goals. They care more about hitting their quarterly goals then customer satisfaction. If you aren't into sales, then banking probably isn't for you. Because even as a teller, you have a sales quota that you need to meet.

advice: Listen to your employees and focus more on people. There is a culture of fear and intimidation within the bank driven by how the bank is run. You did a terrible job laying off people almost weekly throughout the pandemic. All layoffs should have been done at the same time. You should be ashamed of how it was done. People came to work every week wondering if they would still have a job. The people that remained were left to figure out who was still with the bank and who wasn’t because the bank did not communicate the layoffs. What you did was heartless, extremely insensitive, and completely antithetical to the bank’s brand of “respect”. The next time you have to do layoffs, retain the good people and let go of the one that are not.
pros: Great pay, benefits, and lucrative incentive programs.
cons: Lack of empathy/concern for employees, outdated/antiquated systems (1990s), and a cultural that is largely unethical. Senior leadership constantly changes in the bank and there is weak/poor leadership in key upper management roles throughout the bank including new leadership being brought in. The bank lacks diversity as well.

cons: No work life balance.  No training or support for position when promoted.  I worked at SC for 4 years and I had 6 different supervisors.  Four of them were let go - only 1 left on his own.  They do not hire in my experience looking at the big picture of needs only short term goals. My last supervisor had no prior experience for the job and only spent 15 min a week with me. Leadership operates like bullies to it's employees = recipe for failure.

advice: Invest more in your employees - more internal promotion opportunities, chances for less senior team members to network with leadership staff, more cross-department engagement. Revise the employee grade system. Invest in tech, tools, and access to make our jobs easier.
pros: Great potential to make a name for yourself and establish yourself in the Santander network if you’re willing to put yourself out there. All teams are overworked, but allows autonomy and ability to manage your work on your own terms. Work-life balance is easy to maintain, vacation days are generous. If you work hard, compensation will reflect it. Management team is finally moving in the right direction, the consistency is appreciated.
cons: Processes are long, antiquated, convoluted and ineffective - and nearly impossible to innovate. Teams often work in silos and communication can be difficult - magnified by the hierarchical nature of the Bank. Minimize turnover. Develop products even employees want to use.

advice: All of you need to exit on State St. The bank need to be bought/sold and or dismantled. Your bank is not a bank. It's a widget factory. I'm sad I put so much time in there thinking it would get better. The good news? Most leave for better opportunities.

cons: Constant shifting of direction. New CEO comes in and "let's throw this against a wall and see what sticks". They create a culture of fear rather than if teamwork. pros: I apologize - I cannot honestly think of a single one.

Really really inexperienced management (turnover is so high that our EVP of HR was an admin just a couple of years ago).

advice: When a position should be created, do the right thing and interview for job.  Choose the best candidate independently of what HQ will think.
pros: Some good people working hard in the branches and back-offices.
cons:
New opportunities are given to wives, cousins, son-in-law of former CEO and protected people that do not have experience in the areas...Equal Opportunity does not exist in management and specially in senior management.
Lack of leadership: company is constantly trying to figure out what is not working when the problem is almost nothing works well.
Expatriates don't have commitment to fix the company, rather simply to experience US (which they never do).  They come and they go and nothing improves.
Group thinking:  So many committees, but nobody express their opinion, all agree or get shipped away back to Spain.

summary: Pretty great company, good benefits, nice people to work with, really supportive management
advice: my managers have for the most part always been extremely kind, understanding, and rewarding of hard work and years of service
pros: good benefits, great management, opportunities are here if you want to work in banking
cons: there is a persistent demand for sales, which is probably common for all consumer banks. in order to move ahead you have to be very sales driven, if you are it is really a great place to work. if you aren't it is still a great place to work, but you might not move as fast

advice: Get a clue if you don't think sales adds value get rid of them
pros: There is nothing positive working here except to find out what a mismanaged company is.
cons: Leadership is from internal promotions from an Asm to rsm which are not deserved.  Majority is women who are ill equipped and brain washed to manage by intimidation and no industry knowledge.  As an Asm you are treated like a child judged on how many calls and emails you logged that day.  You are subject to canned conference calls about what not to discuss or how to act at a national sales meeting, "no puke breathe, you will show up early and not leave until the event is done".  More or less don't embarrass your rsm.

advice: Quit ripping off customers by charging your insane rates and fees. Make policies consistent across all regions. Take a hard look at yourselves, your peers, your staff and your culture there. Once you do, make a doctor appt. to get prescribed Ambien. If your honest with yourself, you're going to need it to be able to sleep at night.
pros: No pros really. It's a job if you are completely desperate, on drugs (no drug test), have a criminal record, or no moral compass.
cons: No work life balance, immature "managers" who have obvious favorites and will cater to them at your expense, unrealistic goals set by upper management so they can save money in slow months by not paying bonuses, no consistent feedback and what feedback you do receive is if you do something wrong.

advice: stop trying to be every other bank (Chase, Wells, etc.), find what works for your customers and employees. People hate the bank for what it is but stay because of your employees (the rare good ones).
pros: good people, used to have a decent incentive program
cons: management is horrible, upper management doesn't know what they are doing, tries to do 10 things at once and wonders why they all fail, no support, lets quality people go at a drop of a hat but horrible employees somehow stay, just an all around s**t show.

advice: Hire more people so you don't have to force overtime on your employees.
pros:
Get extra pay for travel time as a Float Teller.
Lots of overtime.
Some reimbursement for travel expenses: when traveling far some extra gas money, and/or parking fees
Generally most co-workers are polite and helpful
cons:
No flexibility with scheduling; they tell me which days and hours.
I asked for no overtime and lesser hours and still they overload me with overtime.
During closing duties, many employees are slow so you can get stuck after a branch closes till very late at night.

advice: Dear very wise and elder management, with all due respect to you to whom I bear absolutely no grudge. As none of you won't step aside cause you've been survivor-ly enough so as to reach the top and you won't let it slip it through your fingers at no cost, could you please just take up a very time-consuming hobby and let us move up the ladder?
pros: Outstanding benefits program. The "Financial City" that Santander has set up in Madrid can provide a good deal of benefits to make your life easier while at work: from subsidized kindergarden,to medical facilities with almost any specialist you need. You'll also find a sports facility quite unique with pretty much any sports field you can imagine (including a well-equipped gym). Not to mention the location in the middle of the woods which is quite impressive: walking from building to building (quite a distance sometimes) is less burdensome if you can hear the birds singing meanwhile.
cons:
So: location 10, benefits 10.
The rest just get worse.
Career opportunities are there for whoever wants to take it...and: a) is elder enough or b)has enough high-echelon connections. Ideally, complying with one of the above  will suffice, but complying with both will boost your options. 
After a few years working here, is kind of obvious that Santander and meritocracy are true enemies or, in other words, if you want to raise, you need to act as if you were to survive the company...and whatever the company throws at you.
Which, by the way, is going to make you choke. We are talking of one of the biggest banks in the world so basically profits come first, rest is secondary. That means you are going to have to deal with whatever you've been hired to manage according to your profile, area of expertise and so on...and whatever other random stuff 10 other people are NOT going to be hired to manage. Of course, the area of expertise of such imaginary staff need not to be related to whatever you know how/want/are capable of managing. Bottomline, you'll end up packaging company's food, selling T-shirts, analyzing financial reports, debugging IT customer service software, saying who does what, organizing a bunch of teams' work, drafting Senior Management speeches, mowing the grass, making Senior Management decisions, and even taking a 5 minute standing-still nap in the middle of somewhere. All that for a pay of....too low to be honest. As you may already have inferred work/life balance is non-existent: too cool a location comes with the drawback of being too far away from civilization and if you cross that with the absurd workload you end up spending most of your day there.

summary: Things Could Be So Much Better With Just A Little Effort.
advice: The company desperately needs to do a much better job communicating with employees. We don't even know what direction the company is going in, and we work here. Also, there's needs to be more investment into your people or you risk losing your best and brightest.
pros: Good experience if you're looking to learn about the world of auto lending. Great people. Central location with rail access. Relaxed dress code.
cons: The company is poorly run. Compensation is not up to industry standard. No real growth opportunities. Company does not invest in its own people. Training is a joke

pros: The amount of sick/vacation time they give is great for people just starting with the bank.  Having Sundays off is awesome as well as paid holidays.  A lot of the staff is nice for the most part.  The company does a lot of training's and theres always somewhere you can go to find the answers to your questions
cons: The company is making too many changes all at once.  There are a lot of branches that are short handed due to a lot of people quitting,  The payout plan was changed so everyones making a lot less for bonuses but doing a lot more work.

advice: Stop wasting money on overpaid executives who don't add any value. CEO needs to run company and replace top team with people that get stuff done, like it used to be.
pros: Some really smart and friendly people. Casual dress. Free coffee in headquarters. CEO is a nice guy.
cons: Top leadership all replaced last year. New leadership talk a lot but clueless. Lot of putting out fires instead of planning. The Santander USA CEO in Boston really runs the place now. Used to be a fun place to work but now its like a division of the bank and the bank doesn't know how to run this type of business. Cant trust top management team - say one thing and do another. A lot of the new top execs just care about themselves not the company or associates. Sub-prime lender.

advice:
There is no culture here and until you fix that it, it will continue to impede cohesion and progress.  In other words; you are one semi-major issue away from everything falling apart as there is no loyalty to the company.  

HR and recruitment is a huge impedance and widely disliked by the entire company.  Significant changes are necessary.
pros:
Above average benefits (family leave is definitely a plus)
Ability to telework
Available parking at Dorchester location
cons:
What was promised by the recruiter does not match the reality (compensation, bonus potential, position responsibilities, and many others).  
Difficult to square promised changes by senior management with actual progress.  
No recourse to challenge leadership without significant exposure and risks to personal career viability. 
Compensation levels are generally lower than competitors

advice: hire more tellers, raise the pay rate for tellers and Branch Operations Managers, Not only is the Branch Operations responsible for Operations, they are the backup when the Branch Manager is on PTO or out of the office
pros: medical benefits are good eye care benefit is excellent , staff is friendly
cons: they cut the staff in the branches on the teller side way to short, i work a lot of days by myself without being able to get any break , they focus on bringing in bankers to bring in revenue, but they need to focus on staffing the teller side, that will improve their customer service

advice: Treat and appreciate your employees the way you expect them to treat and appreciate the customers. As leaders, consider the tone you’re setting and the environment you’re creating for agents. Giving agents misinformation instead of looking into the issue only leads to more problems.
pros: Decent pay with bonuses. Generous PTO.
cons: Management is very unprofessional and lazy. They never want to help or do their job. No coaching available and the only communication you get is when you’re already being written up. Agents in other departments are allowed to be rude and make the job more difficult. Lack of training and a ton of misinformation.

advice: learn to value good employees, treat your employees well and they will treat your customers well and you will have higher revenue and production.  keep in mind Sir Richard Branson's quotes-"“Train people well enough so they can leave, treat them well enough so they don’t want to.” and “Clients do not come first. Employees come first. If you take care of your employees, they will take care of the clients.”
pros: not many pros, if and when company meets goal will you receive a decent bonus if you are in the top 10 in your department
cons: no advancement, can work there for years and not be able to move due to intercompany politics. no longer making the revenue needed to receive good bonuses(mostly because SCUSA no longer values their employees over their shareholders)

advice: Upper management needs to monitor their regional managers and see how they treat their employees. Also don't change bonus structure every 12 months.
pros: Great co workers, loved working from home. Company pays well and fun national sales meetings. They had pretty good benefits too.
cons: My manager was a micromanager. She was always monitoring me closely and always checking in with me even though I was one of the top performers. She hires a lot of her friends or relatives but she even fired one of her relatives. There are currently two managers over the team now. You want the him,not the her.

advice: You are missing good people. People who love to work in this company. People who never were adivised about possible failure. New manager who are not engaged with the company are deciding important thing about the company, but they are not really interested in the company's future.
pros: The company provide huge benefit, an average salary for the majority and if you have the opportunity to work in specific areas there possibilities to achieve high positions.
cons: The manager changes are often, this way every time the employee have to prove their worth for a new boss. Every year lots of people are fired to reduce the costs.

advice: Stop listening to lies. Open your eyes to what is really going on. Listen to your managers when they tell you they need something.
pros: They talk like they care about the employees but they don't
cons: If you are not in the "club" you will not go anywhere. Managers have no support. AVPs and SVPs don't give you any time. You tell them what you need and they don't listen. Directors are so far disconnected thet don't know what is going on. HR is a Joke they don't help anyone. All you get is lies and backstabbing. Don't trust anyone there. Systems and processes are out dated and nobody knows what is going on. Their moto is if you see something say something but when you so be prepared for the back lash. They will make your life miserable.

summary: I have worked for Santander for almost 5 years. Over the last two years I have served as an AVP.
advice: Treat your staff the way you would want yo be treated. Allow them to preform their job titles without being micromanaged. Lead by example not fear. "People quit bosses, not jobs"
pros: Interaction with peers and staff, ability to learn other areas of the business.
cons: The pay is not competitive with the current market, no consistency, executive management can be bullies from time to time, not a knowledge bases company, it's more about who you know. Work life balance can be nonexistent in certain departments

summary: Working at Santander Consumer was an eye opener. My time there was a living nightmare that I wish to never relive.
advice: Be a manager not a friend. Hire managers with people skills people who deserve the position.
pros: Pay rate was fair. 401k plan wasn't bad.
cons: Working in the Funding Dept is like being in high school. They treat you like production workers, your just a number. You only get promoted to a position if your in the certain clique. The amount of gossip and malicious bullying is sad. I've watched numerous great employees go from top to bottom. Their mental and physical health deteriorate when they reached out to HR for help they were attacked worse. To the point they let them go. Management watched it all from the beginning. Some were even part of it.

advice: Stay in your position for more than a months time before jumping from one bank to another.
pros: I worked with a great team, everyone was friendly, had easy traffic coming in to branch daily. It was a full-time position and there was growth opportunities.
cons: HUGE turnover in employees and management changes all the time. Monthly it seemed like. Goals became ridiculous for you to achieve them and if you did, they would investigate why you were able to make those goals and do anything to sabotage or prevent you from earning a bonus, which honestly was not much.

summary: Six day work weeks, unfair pay practices, decent brand
advice:
Give EVERYONE the same starting pay. People talk, always. Plus there are great sites like Glassdoor to make sure everyone knows what everyone else earns.

LESS EMAILS! Take “Under the wire” out of your vocabulary. 

FIVE DAY WORK WEEKS!!! Tell folks they can get overtime for volunteering to work Sundays. That’s how most banks do it. 

Close at 5. For your customers.

Stop trying to sell your employees on “get out of work early” on call nights. It’s a punishment. We all know it.
pros:
Ask for at least $15 an hour or you’ll regret it. And I’m one of the best in my district, regularly!! Of course, they did send me a shout out : / 

Paid days off from day one....just don’t quit before you have been there long enough to ‘earn’ them or you’ll be billed for them.

Lots of turnover, so there’s hope you’ll be able to grab more sales in between new recruits.

Paid training.
cons:
I was not told that we would be working six day work weeks, every single week, with a FEW exceptions. I was told the reverse. Most of the people at the company leave, very high turnover. Also, TONS AND TONS of excessive emails, daily. Miss one with something important? You are screwed. Don’t reach a goal for Investment Appoints? You have to stay late, on top of only having one day off a week! Some people save new account openings and don’t process them so that they can ‘put them on’ to get out of staying late. Not too fair to the honest employees who want to help customers in a timely matter.

I was hired at well below the average rate. I found this out at training in Harrisburg, Pa. Everyone that was hired around me, in the same district, makes up to $17 an hour! Staying late and not reaching quarterly goal payouts makes this really hurt. I know that others are making more than me, every single six day week they put in.

Their latest sales mantra is Simple Easy Fair or something similar. Just rolling out. Well, the computer program is the worst I’ve ever seen. Yes, they seem to be tweaking it constantly, but that also adds to confusion. You need to click dozens of times to do the most simple of things. Their system is NOT user friendly.

As of November of this year, they plan to have every single customer-facing employee become a Universal Banker. This means everyone in every branch will be competing for new accounts and investment appointments so that they can make quarterly payout. That means, you guessed it, sales competition, backstabbing, working even more hours so you don’t miss your chance to close someone. I’m already seeing it. They don’t seem to realize this will cause so much more stress in the branches. They hide it behind a few things. Choreography. That means you get the first person to come in, someone else goes to lobby in your place and get the next person, and around and around we go. Well, you’re pretty screwed most of the time and in so many scenarios. Who wants to work like that? If I did, I’d sell cars.  

They also hide it behind mentioning the “positive” which is that every employee can do everything. Open an account (bonus money!), do teller transactions (no extra money), close accounts (no extra money), etc etc.

Santander is BIG on coming up with negatives and trying to say them in a positive way. We are no longer going to be offering the X20 account, that can pay customers $20 a month, every single month. Oh, that’s positive! Six day work weeks! Oh, Saturdays don’t count because we are only going to be there for  HALF A DAY. Universal Banker so more Feet On The Street! Oh, leave the branch and risk losing a walk-in? More competition? 

You get the idea.

advice: You may bring in new 'leaders'.  Still putting a pretty bandage over the boo boo underneath.  Sound like politic?  Big time!
pros: I am giving the Bank 2 stars.  1 for the good colleagues and 1 for pay scale.  The bank employs some good people.  Unfortunately, they are the ones who leave or driven out.
cons: Who is left?  The ones who have no place else to go.  There is no process and procedure in place.  No one wants to take ownership.  Staff perform work that could be avoided if management would listen and enforce.  oh well...

advice: Appreciate your employees more and listen to them. Do not try to micromanage and do not put up with childish management tantrums or high school type cliques.
pros:
The benefits and compensation were excellent, and a yearly bonus that was most welcome. They did fun little employee activities for one week a year and gave little gifts though very inexpensive were very appreciated.

Many of not most of the people that work there are very friendly and good at their jobs and decent to work with.

The actual office is new and nice (as of 2016) and there are machines offering a great many choices of free coffee.
cons:
There is a severe lack of proper process when it comes to projects and what is most important. 

Though management is typically nice they are not always attentive or understanding. I recall one incident where while working from home I logged off before I read an email sent a little after 5, which is when my day ended, and I was then texted, emailed, and called multiple times till I was able to pick up and was accused of leaving early and threatened with being demoted to contractor (something not possible or even within that managers power to do) and when I addressed this behavior to my superior no action was taken as far as I could tell. This happened at least three times from the same manager.

It's a very clique ish environment and if you don't fit the a great deal of trash talk will happen behind your back, just like in high school.

There was a lack of appreciation and even understanding of the jobs that were done. For mine in particular, I rarely got a thank you beyond my one or two coworkers and a great deal of complaining when any little thing may not be in its perfect place. Also I was forced to repeat myself many many time to my own team why certain thing last couldn't be done or shouldn't be done as if they didn't believe me or trust me.

advice: The company needs to be overhauled b/c changing a few things here and there won't help the mentality.
pros: Fair pay. They match 6% of your 401K contribution (percentange may have gone down now). Some people can work from home.
cons:
Incompetent executives, very secretive. They hire a lot of Indians, and prefer to hire men over women.  Some of the managers are very unprofessional, lying and backstabbing, and create a hostile environment. Can't trust anyone. If you see ethical violations or even non-compliance with a regulation or a law and speak up, they will mark you and call you a troublemaker. If you complain to HR, you will be retaliated against extensively, until you quit or they fire you.

While I met good people there, it's the bad apples that spoil the bunch. A lot of bad apples.

pros: I loved every bit of working at Santander and I wish they would hire me back,  I came to work did what I was supposed to do and more,  overall experience with them is a 10
cons: I disliked the day that my entire team was split up and we got a new manager

advice: Keep up the positive work atmosphere.
pros:
Working at Santander has been one of the best career changes I’ve made.  I truly enjoy going to work each day and feel appreciated for all I do.

1. Competitive pay.  Ability to earn more through bonuses.
2. Ample PTO!  Plus volunteer pto, developmental pto. 
3.  Health insurance is great and affordable.
4. 6% 401k match in 2020. 
5. Every single person I’ve dealt with from training facilitators, tech support, branch employees, and district executives have all been so positive and appreciative.  It’s a wonderful atmosphere.
cons: I honestly can’t think of one.

advice: Make people be accountable for their roles and responsibilities so people can own their work.
pros: Slightly above average benefits for the Boston area, dynamic workplace with many changes and potential for movement due to size and new opportunities.
cons: With many changes comes much uncertainty and lack of structure.  If you want things in black and white, this is not the right environment for you.  If however you enjoy a challenge and willing to get your hands dirty, this is a great place to get your hands dirty and gain valuable experience for your resume in a corporate/banking setting.

summary: Good place to start your career, but if you are ambitious and want to grow far professionally not the right place
advice:
Empower and motivate talent giving them more responsibilities
Make a better use of your STEP managers and stop using them as interns for 3 years
pros:
Multinational; good opportunities to work abroad: STEP program (3 years abroad, 2 countries), MUNDO program (3-5 months in Spain generally)
Lots of work
cons:
Too hierarchical
Senior executives want to be treated like gods
Very snobby
you will not get very far without having a good friend or family member in the top
You will not have too many responsibilities if you are young, even if you are a top performer
Your career will slow down considerably after 5-7 years

advice:
- PAY PEOPLE WHAT THEY DESERVE. If someone starts as a teller at, for example 14.50 or even 16.50  and gets promoted to Operations MANAGER, they should not get paid only a couple bucks more. MINIMUM is probably 25/hour for the amount of work that goes into it!
- If the turnover rate is so bad, there's a real REAL reason for it! Ask your employees what THE COMPANY can do for them instead of continuously pushing for them to give the company more and more.
pros:
- Learned A LOT about what it means to be a manager
- Small bank so I was able to know everyone that worked within the same district as me
- DIVERSE employees. Loved having co-workers of different backgrounds
- Easily able to move up. 
- Plenty of banking knowledge given
- Extremely talented people work there. You will find life friends and inspiration people (in branches).
cons:
- There were times I was not able to have LUNCH BREAK (which is against the law btw) because the turnover rate in my district was HORRIBLE. Even though they have "float staff" that go around helping branches, NO ONE came to help. I had to contact HR in order to FINALLY have the float manager send someone to my branch so I could take a break after having told him I needed someone!
- When I worked under short-staffed conditions and had to maintain the teller line all by myself with no break when the manager was on PTO (I was second in command so when the manager is on PTO, I'm the manager), I got sick and had to call out the next day. The District Executive ended up reprimanding me for calling out! MAYBE if you cared about your employees and send adequate help, I wouldn't have gotten sick from being overworked and NOT GETTING A LUNCH BREAK! 
- If you run out of Paid Time Off (PTO), you cannot even call out sick. Having to call out sick should not be something that can be held against an employee. Especially if you have a doctors note. 
- The medical benefits are a joke.
- The way HR handles severe situations is a joke, they only care about covering the company. 
-My pay for all the work I did was 100% not enough. I was GROSSLY underpaid!   
-NO work-life balance. NONE.

summary: For my position in the bank it’s been great
advice: The key and combo log is so redundant and was obviously not created by someone that ever worked in a branch. To assign 2 keys you have to get 10 signatures/initials. Now imagine setting up a new team member that will have 11 keys and at least 5 combos.
pros: I have a great team, when coronavirus happened we were given an additional $50 every day we worked, a lot of PTO, summer events, commission, health care/dental, Charles Schwab 401k, tuition reimbursement program, volunteer PTO
cons: The systems are definitely out dated, HR department is not the best, currently making a lot of cuts to jobs, a lot of redundant paperwork and check lists, policy’s are constantly changing

summary: Branches are failing due to lack of support and leadership from higher ups.
advice: Instead of looking at branch team members and wonder why the branches are failing. It’s time to look higher up the ladder and notice the people who fail to give the branches the support they desperately need. Tellers and UOS’s are usually over worked and underplayed while Bankers and managers rarely work and make all the money. It got very toxic this last year with Covid. I don’t see them getting better any time soon.
pros: Made some amazing friends. Met some nice people being at the branch.
cons:
Over worked
Not enough pay
Treated like you are replaceable 
DE does not help branches that need help but is quick to be upset if we don’t have high scores.

advice: Stop wasting $ on flyers and buckslips, invest it in upgrading/replacing your painful technology.  Upper management should get their visions on the same page, and open up the lines of communication.  Stop instructing your employees to apologize for inconveniences caused by system issues, these are unacceptable.
pros: Since the district is so under-staffed, you get to know employees from other locations pretty well - and we all support each other.
cons: Technology is a nightmare.  Turnover is always occurring company-wide.  Seems like a new idea/process is implemented every other month and either doesn't work or never actually happens.  System improvements lead to quirks somewhere else.  "Coming soon" never arrives.  Oh and then there's the "known issues" and the "glitches".

summary: Stay Away!! Check your morals and experience at the door. You won't need them here. Just fall in line.....or else!!
advice: Time to shake the apple tree. Top to bottom. That's what this place needs, but it won't happen. You need to take this down to the studs and rebuild.
pros: There's plenty of opportunities due to multiple shifting priorities. However you will run into multiple roadblocks in getting anything accomplished. There are a lot of people TRYING to do the right thing and who take pride in their jobs.
cons: Company is riddled with cover ups, willful blindness, and corruption. Your integrity will be challenged at this company.  If you do not fall in line they will make your life miserable. The technology and infrastructure is reminiscent of 1980 and EVERYTHING in this company is performed manually. It is nearly impossible to complete daily tasks due to the slowness/lack of system availability.

advice: If they are going to "coach" employees, then advice them on how to succeed, do not just look at the lack of sales and move on.
pros: Goals could be easily met if you work in a wealthy community
cons: Unrealistic goals and expectations. They do not treat their employees well. Constant "coaching" which does not help and interferes with time with customers (which interferes with your sales.) One minor mistake and they withhold your commission for that quarter, especially if you stand to make a lot of money.  Not a good work-life balance. If you are lacking in sales, you have to go to stores and offices to find new customers, sometimes on your own time and without receiving expenses.
