pros: Greats exposure to Capital Markets
cons: Lack of growth for department

summary: Needs major improvement with their values.
advice: Listen to your associates please stop running off good employees. Please stop allowing upper management AVP's and direct managers to bully associates and get away with it. The company says all doors are open for us to speak with someone but if we do we will be wrote up for something "they found". Look into why the turnover rate is so high employees are miserable here. This place used to be an amazing company to work for not anymore.
pros: Good pay good bonus structure when management does not feel the need to steal it from you.
cons: This company will retaliate against you the second you voice your opinion.

summary: The Bank is in state of chaos; if they don't pass CCAR and other reg exams they will be forced to close down.
advice: Stop trying to implement so many dramatic and quick changes all of a sudden. Stop relaying on 20 year old external consultants to save the bank. Take a step bank and understand what the problems and how to solve them.  Madrid must step up and stop this carnage.
pros: Sitting on your as all day texting friends and family.   Job security was great until Mr Powell arrived and with him came the culture of slashing jobs to save costs... Why doesn't he and his entourage take a salary cut and preach by example.
cons:
Wasting 6 years of your life in a bank like this.  
HR is truly abysmal, they recently reshuffled key personnel but what they brought in is worst.
After 6 years at the Boston HQ, the true inability of high level management to create an environment where one can make a difference and where talent is appreciated.
The blend of Spanish and American style leadership has not worked; attrition rate is out of control; fragmentation in the teams and corporate spirit is low; salaries are about 25% below the competition; and above all everyone is trying to save their own ases and there is not sense of team. And wrap this up in a setting where databases and access to reliable data sources are archaic or none existent; hundreds of 20 year old consultants are running the bank and drafting key regulatory documents.. And one wonders, what is the use of having all these super well paid chief risk officers, SVPs, EVPs... currently sitting in their offices and reading through recycled power points.
Final advice:  this is a sinking ship, stay away. Bank will be forced to close down in one year.

advice: Get it together
pros: Santander's team members have always been its strength.  However, many, many talented people have left or been pushed out.
cons: Too many to list really.  The ineffective leadership is primary though.  There is no vision, decisions seem to be made on a knee jerk basis and often reversed months later when another leadership shuffle happens.  The bank has been continuously declining for the last few years.  Employees are unhappy and have lost confidence in the organization.

advice: Define a strategy and a roadmap, define priorities and important tasks that add value, get rid of waste in unnecessary reports, committees, etc..
pros: Good benefits, solid global bank
cons: My manager had no direction, likes to micromanage and asked for things he later denied. Everything is urgent and there is no strategic roadmap to where the bank needs to go and how, lack of priorities is frustrating. This is common in the group

summary: Great place to begin your banking career
advice: Hire more people with banking backgrounds and lead by example.  It would be nice to see management lead by example by having a more professional appearance and let go of the clique-y behavior.
pros:
Laid back work environment
Promote from within
On-the-job training
cons:
The systems are out dated and in-efficient.  Santander could provide a better colleague and customer experience with a serious investment in the technological aspect of the call center.

Management leave much to be desired along the professionalism aspect.

summary: Not paying enough but wants more from employees
advice: They need to pay more attention to what their employees are saying and make Santander an enjoyable place for their workers and that will make a difference and their customers will notice and appreciate it.
pros: Some coworkers makes it worthwhile to work in the bank.
cons: Their policy and procedures contradict itself and others like it. They need to fix it so all employees can be on the same page. They don’t treat their employees with RESPECT like they advertise

summary: Good Company  to work  at  with  no experience  good training
advice: if you have a good  employee , let them  know  about if they feel ready  to  take over  a new  higher position,  and don't  do favoritisms
pros: company trains you to avoid failure , chance to advance in to company , good salary , work hard for extra bonus
cons: management should notice more good working employees , instead of favoritisms

summary: Some great people, some terrible bureaucrats
advice: Trim down all the paper pushers and red-tape and get the best people doing the job. Change the big organisational structures that create conflicting goals between those internal organisations, which in turn leads to resistance against change (i.e. resistance against actually doing anything)
pros: Great work location in Madrid, although out of the city. Work campus is beautiful with good restaurants. Some very friendly and clever people working there.
cons: Late hours working culture, and mired in crazy non-nonsensical bureacracy

advice:
Pick a direction for the company (service v. sales) and stick to it!
Create a management development program to both attract top talent from outside and prepare future leaders from within,
pros: Great incentive potential, upward mobility, real team environment
cons:
Company's priorities change too often, leaving many old timers at odds with the new regime and many mixed messages. 
Company can at times out of tune with the rest of the industry, too slow to adapt to changes

advice: Bring back Kaplan classes for those taking licensing exams and give trainees more time to prepare. Also, update the training modules online!
pros: Nice co-workers, good environment, benefits, decent base pay.
cons: Overwhelming workload initially. In the first month, you are expected to keep up with a study calender while also going through all the training modules online. Unless you have a background in finance, learning the material for the FINRA exams in such a short period of time is very difficult. Would've been nice to do the training modules at orientation.

advice: Train the Branch Managers better, half of them do not know what they are doing. That makes it harder for them UOS to get work done. Example,  when a branch manager cannot open accounts or can't open a teller box because of no knowledge of how to, so they just sit back and watch .
pros:
if you are willing to learn new things it will help get career advancement. 
PTO is great
cons:
Management needs better training
Every district needs to be on the same page
Incentive could be better

summary: It was a first nice work experience, I was employed in the financial markets department where i was perfectly mentored.
advice: May be create some kind of trainee programs within the lisbon office as short term interships are not as productive as they should
pros: Good support from the financial market team, flexible schedule and opportunity to establish good contacts and relations with the several investors
cons: sometimes the work was a bit repetitive and the workload was not well distributed as a consequence of the economic situation we are living nowadays

advice: Keep track of where branch clients are doing their banking and fine tune the call lists based on branch to client activity
pros: Good work environment with excellent training and mentoring.  Easy work schedule and a good place to learn client management skills in a multi faceted work environment
cons: The commission on sales performed by an outside financial advisor were low. It was not always easy to meet with clients to discuss financial objectives as many clients do not visit the bank but instead do their banking online

pros:
One of the biggest banks in Europe and Worldwide. 
International Opportunities 
Good work-life balance. 
If you are in Madrid HQ and have schedule flexibility, you can enjoy the gym and practice other sports.
cons: In the end your are working for a retail bank, and management focuses on developping this segment. Global Banking & Markets (which is like IB for Santander) is going through a review and is not considered key, so think about it if you want to pursue an IB career. I would not recommend starting in Santander

summary: Growing, lots of opportunity but really fast paced.
pros: People are wonderful, friendly, engaging and smart.  Lots of opportunity to create processes and procedures.  Wonderful events for Associates and their families.
cons: Formerly a small company, transitioning into a mid-sized organization, there are a variety of growing pains.  The company leadership is working to make this happen while maintaining it's small company feel.  This is a difficult challenge resulting in what feels like a lack of communication and last-minute decisions.  Change is communicated in the moment - it's definitely a ride!

advice: Treat your employees as you want to be treated.  Without them, your bank doesn't run and no, they aren't easily to replace, especially certain departments.
pros: Company has decent pay, good benefits (all the Bank holidays too).  Company seems to be trying to take a better interest in their employees, implementing flexiworking, among other things.
cons: Company talks the talk, but doesn't walk the walk.  Difficult to get raises/promotions as an existing employee, so do your best negotiating before you walk through the door.

advice: Listen to your employees and make them feel heard.
pros: Great team and learning environment. Great 401k benefits. Flexible hours. Casual dress. WFH day. Good commute. Yearly bonus. Raise every 6 months. SCUSA supports career exploration. Asks for employees input.
cons: Under paid. Management knows this but doesn't do anything about it. Below average PTO. No paternity/maternity leave. The company keeps under performing employees that hinder Productivity. Very "I want it yesterday" attitude. Terrible processes. Asks for employee input but doesn't apply them.

advice: Upgrade Technology
pros: Colleagues and wondering when another bank will purchase this bank. The color red. Taking a lunch break.  Going on vacation
cons: Technology is so far behind its hard to do your job. Branch Operations are behind 15 + years, Online Banking never works, systems go down in the middle of transactions and the amount of time the system takes to complete a transaction is back in typewriter days. Instead of fixing technology, the focus is on customer service when the customers don't have the tools and other banks offer to streamline their banking. You get the same Leads to call customers and hound them for business because a lot of people never heard of the bank.

summary: Fast pace company with growing pains
advice: Santander was a better company before it went public.
pros: Benefits are not bad.  The company tries to focus on good benefits for the employees.  They do offer opportunity for advancement.
cons: They are in the process of C-Level change with a company wide shake down.  Gets very stressful due to this type of environment.  The open floor/desk  is a nightmare because you hear every conversation and have no privacy.  You are sitting 2 feet away from others.

advice: Keep up the communication
pros:
Global company with cool brand
Fair pay and benefits
Great culture emerging under new leadership
cons: Things are busy.  YOu have to be ready to grab a shovel and pitch in to a turn around effort

advice: Clean house in management and HR and get some new blood.
pros: they finally are giving us more than 2 weeks vacation.
cons:
They've laid off a lot of really good people to keep the low paid employees.
They say they are trying to make it a better place to work but the really bad and mean managers are still in charge and the really bad leadership in HR is still there.

advice: more staff, overlook the managemanet, listen to empoyers.
pros: Work life i freindly everyone knows each other in the distrist. You will have areas of oppurtunites to learn and grow. A very well organzied coaching programs to help with the your role. There is no daily pressure.
cons: Based on who your District excutive  and manager is there is limited growth. Alot of short staffing issue will hold your growth in the company.

advice: Headquarters needs to take a good look at the entire title management team & do a complete work over. The employees are people. We’re not just numbers. Titles department feels like a sweat shop
pros: It’s a paycheck until s better job comes along
cons: Too many team leads & managers. Micromanaging at its finest. Can’t use the restroom without letting a manager know. Specific break & lunch times.  ABP walks around & watches everything you are doing. AVP doesn’t allow you to talk to your neighbors. Manage my team looks down & belittles the employees who actually work for a paycheck! Very stressful environment. Let people do their jobs!

advice: Continue to work on keeping up with technology to adhere to employees and customers satisfaction.
pros: Employee focus, they prioritize making sure the new hires have a smooth transition with the training programs. They treat everyone nice and fairly it does not matter if you been here for a day they make you feel welcome and valued.
cons: Just have to be patience with the technology its a bit slow, however they are working on making updates.

summary: Don’t work here if you have self respect
advice: Care about your employees more, don’t try to force them to do unethical things, don’t hire outside the company when you have people in the branch you could promote to better jobs.
pros: They hire pretty much anyone, have decent benefits.
cons: So many downsides. Probably the worst work environment I’ve ever had. They “accidentally” cut my pay and then called me a liar when I provided proof, tried to get me to open accounts for customers without their knowledge to boost sales, and forced me to work 6 days a week and didn’t pay me overtime by having me take extended lunch breaks.

advice: Covid isn’t going anywhere, variants will continue to pop up especially with all the unvaccinated people in TX. Stop with the power play and let non location dependent depts. continue  working from home
pros: Pay and proximity to my house
cons: CEO Tim Wennes is determined to put everyone’s health at risk by forcing people to return to the office. There is no reason for non-location dependent depts. to be in the office. Considering we literally sit on top of each other in an unventilated warehouse where a majority of people are on the phone all day and can’t be masked I fully expect a covid outbreak to happen.

summary: Lots of bureaucracy  and lots of turnover.
advice: Stop burning people out and address the high turnover rate.
pros: There are some good people working there and the benefits are good.
cons: There are a ton of processes that must be adhered to, and with many of the groups in Mexico or Spain, navigating the bureaucracy is difficult. The hours are long and you are expected to work at all hours. The turnover is very high.

pros: Since you multitask and participate in so many projects there is a big opportunity to learn

advice: define a clear strategy for IBD and a career development plan for employees
pros:

- One of the biggest banks in Latam

summary: this place just isn't what it used to be

pros: Good pay for people they want.  Great work/life balance as long as you are producing.
cons: Promoting unqualified employee who are their "boys".  Senior management is changing compensation in order not to pay their employees.  Leadership is missing.  People are just going in and out of the bank.

pros: The benefits, sick time, vacation time, bonus structure, culture, values, pay grade, hours and supervisors are all great.

pros: You meet GREAT people at this company and the pay is great also
cons: The cons are its hard to get a bonus if you're not a truly competitive person. It's also hard to get promoted. At this company, it's who you know and not your skills

summary: Good place to work - not flawless, but no copany is
advice: Just get it all more organized.

cons: Awful hiring process. The way business lines are organized is a bit messy, you can get frustrated with that. Sometimes official communication says things which never get to happen.

summary: Company is in denial....even after several chiefs leave
advice: Start looking for better leaders to turn the company around....and fast.....you will continue losing the talent you have until you get better leadership.
pros: Great people, flexible hours and fair pay.
cons: HR is a nightmare, esp when it comes to internal transfers or promotions. They cap the max pay increases for promotions, which sucks the life and motivation out of employees. advice: Change the PTO policy to include increasing amount and how it accrues. 2 weeks is not normal for the market. Evaluate what people actually do and see if it is necessary.
pros: Santander Consumer is growing but they do more to show that they care for their employees more  than other employers. Culture is laid back and non-formal. Pay is good.
cons:
Vacation time off  is only 2 weeks.
Downtown location
Very Cliquish
Feels like a car sales floor or fraternity than a business 
Lots of people doing very little or no work

advice: Stop blaming the BMs and DMs for the problems and look at your process. This is a financial institution not a college football team.
pros: Good benefits, good pay, good products
cons: Sales is the #1 priority here, just the language has changed since WF got all the media attention. Management is consistently "hiring ahead" to keep the doors open to its branches.

advice: Engage with your employees more and truly buy in to the team. Let them know you are on there side. You are there manager but you are for them and you are here to teach them and train them and help them in any way. We do a good Job of this so far but we need to get better.
pros: Fantastic opportunity to not only grow but advance in the company.
cons: Lack of follow up, inconsistency. We tend to say one thing and do another.

advice: I would advice to management to pay more attention to what employers say, since it is important to keep your staff happy in the company.
pros: Good opportunities for people with little experience, good compensation, I like the working environment, since it is quite attractive and the situation of the headquarters
cons: The career opportunities most times do not depend on your performance but on the amount of time you have been working in the company.

pros: Pay is Fair. Monthly bonus payouts, friendly staff,  casual dress code. Health benefits, vision, dental, immediately when you are hired. 120hrs of PTO automatically when hired. You can also but up to additional 40hrs of PTO during annual benefits enrollment. Overtime offered frequently.
cons: next to impossible to have consecutive days off. You will work either a Saturday or Sunday every week. Shift change once a year (bid). Raises rarely happen. Work/ home life balance could improve.

pros: Benefits along with decent pay scale.
cons: Since going public (every year, month and even day) everything about your job title appears to change. Even your pay... New leadership on the Director & VP roles is greatly recommended.  Management, higher-ups & the "Old Headz" are all on the buddy system. If you're not one of them, "I feel bad for you son, I got 99 problems but" this company ain't one - Jay Z.

summary: Fair base, and good earning potential. BUT...
pros: RB position here has pretty fair starting base if you come in licensed. ~50k + bonuses. 5-10k in bonus is more than achievable.
cons: Much of your success relies on location, ability and knowledge of your business partners (Financial Consultants, Mortgage Officer, etc.), and leadership of direct manager. Strive to learn more and be proactive, this can be a great start to a career.

advice: Listen to your average person not just management. Handle the people doing illegal things so you don’t get a fine.
pros: There’s a lot of room for advancement and managers that are looking to mentor you if you’re willing to put in the work. The benefits are decent, but not spectacular.
cons: The pay is abysmal. HR is friends with management and they go out to dinner together. They protect managers that are literally doing illegal things

advice: Give merit raises to team members to encourage them to stay.
pros:
Decent base pay for the amount of experience required to get the job.
Decent benefits.
A large company that isn't going away anytime soon.
Backed by Banco Santander.
A guaranteed paycheck.
cons:
Recruiters exaggerate bonus structures leading you to think you will be paid more than you actually get.
Rigid HR that isn't willing to budge in extenuating circumstances.
No tuition reimbursement. 
No raises unless you get a promotion.
Company changes priorities daily.

advice:
Communication, needed ASAP
Only move on to the next changes after you get positive feedback from the department's Managers.
pros:
Some Awesome employees, wasted in what could be a good bank.
Some very nice employees, a lot neutral and some not so nice.
cons:
They do whatever the head office in Spain tells them to do.
Changing the internal software, but doesn't fix the problems, just moves on to the next department.
Zero communication at all levels.

summary: Too political and big lack of investment in the Branch.
advice: I would not have accepted the position if I had to do it over again.
pros: A small office environment. A number of people have long-term experience there and have been helpful.
cons: Small office environment. No investment in people or the branch. There is a lack of staffing in key areas with no career path. If you are not from Spain you are at a disadvantage. Very bureaucratic and political. Lack of raises since 2008. None of the senior management are all imports that stay for a few years and go back to Madrid so they have no stake.

summary: excellent workplace full of energy and professional people.
advice: Take better career of work life balance and help employees reach their personal goals, provide better incentives to remain on a long term.
pros: This company is well managed and knows its strengths and weaknesses. The vision is clear and there is fluid communication between areas.
cons: Technology is far from where it should be, there are still many obsolete practices and development methodologies are archaic, infrastructure is still lagging.

advice: Stay the course.  Don't roll out new programs/business lines before infrastructure and employees are ready to handle them the right way.
pros: Friendly co-workers, fair pay and incentives.  Expectations were reasonable.  Casual dress code.  Managers seemed to really care about your happiness and development.
cons: Fast growth had its share of hurdles.  Pace could be frantic at times.  Became more rigid and old-school corporate as time went on.

summary: Not compliant with other banks' environment
advice: Maybe the key is to wipe out unnecessary (whole) structures, not pruning the edges from healthy twigs
pros: Since it is still an organization with many improvements to be put in place, growing in a fast-paced fashion is a possibility using the correct skills (more people than technical ones)
cons: Meritocracy is not the prevailing and ultimate feature of the company. Basically, the bank fails to recognize and grasp the talents within the organization. International exchange experiences (short and long term) for a worldwide company is also a point to be improved

summary: I gained a lot of experience but it is difficult to advance unless you someone higher up.
advice: Develop programs where employees can explore other attributes or skills in the industry.
pros: Great experience and the place helped me learn a lot about the business. The environment is mostly friendly. Management tends to engaged with the rest of the floor. The possibility of advancing creates good opportunities to really do well.
cons: You may be stuck in one role for quite sometime. The system may need upgrading as most are asked to do a lot with old software and hardware.

advice: Listen to the lower echelons and "doers" instead of "managers" to identify the solutions to problems.  Encourage dissent and different views on problem resolution.
pros: Large organization with some excellent people to work with and learn from/with.  Decent benefits and pay.
cons: Major disconnect between management in the US and overseas, US leaderships vs Foreign leadership.  Limited opportunities to advance or change career direction unless part of a special group.  Too often the organization creates it's own problems and hurdles and has to run around putting out fires on a daily basis.

advice: Please provide feedback to the candidates for whom you are calling for interviews. Your one feedback can keep the candidates motivated no matter you select them or not.
pros: Not sure , if any
cons:
Very bad experience as got called for interview and got selected. Then again called for 3 more rounds and got a positive feedback and they told they will call me in 1 week. After that i had send so many emails just to ask for the status and provide the feedback but did not get a single response. 
Really bad .

advice: Train the team leads better, get rid of toxic people who bring down moral.
pros: Great co workers,  good benefits, good upper management. Lots of swag given to employees.
cons: Most of the team leads are horrible.  Once you get in a rhythm with a manger they force you to switch teams, they are not all equal. Mandatory over time. Closed down Denver site and immediately started going after people to lower the amount of people who would get severance.  It’s very easy to begin to hate  this job after a while.

advice: Credit resources should be matched to business goals.  In 2014, in order to beef up compliance,a lot of open credit recs were closed, creating a significant stress on credit risk.
pros:
Hard work and intelligence is rewarded. 
Good Management team in the commercial bank segment (middle market specifically)
Bank is working towards improving employee satisfaction
cons:
Re-orgs annually/lots of Sr. management changes (all the time)
Haven't figured out clear strategy on how to succeed in the commercial banking space (strategy has changed significantly over the last three years)
Credit is not necessarily rewarded well; over-time is welcome

advice: Be nice to your employees, they are very good at what they do.
pros: The high level executives know how to grow as a company. This bank is well managed from Spain with very good support in the US.  This is a well managed bank. Conservative approach to banking.  Well trained executives with good reputations.  Excellent management training program if you can get into it. It is competitive.
cons: The pay is not that high in the mortgage lending department, but the training is very good.

advice: Less emphasis on teller referrals and sales. We are told to go on the street soliciting accounts. I didn't think as a Teller manager that I had to act almost as a door to door salesman.
pros: Good people, holidays off, growing bank with new opportunities on the horizon
cons: Sales is more important that operations. As a teller or BOM, you are on the hook for not meeting your goals.. but recieve minimal praise for being operationally sound. Raises were offensively miniscule. You only make money through sales bonuses rather than raises

pros: Had decent health care at the time, and pay out if you reached them.. good paid time off, and able to carry over a week or less if you didnt use it. potiential growth, but a fairly decent place to start your career in banking.
cons: can get stuck with working with old school banking folks that totally disregard all things current (sales process etc) because they have been with santander/sovereign for so long, and dont care about anyone but themselves, rather than working as a team so everyone can benefit.

summary: Improves growth/profits/CX. Corp Finance expertise-Debt, Equity, M&A. MBA Stern S. NYU Fulbright. US resident Green Card
advice: Maintain the Strategic transformational focus in Digitalization, Provide optimal Customer Experience, Increase Customer links with the Bank and continuous Efficiency improvement with a well-diversified and balanced geographical footprint
pros:
Great Customer focus
Multinational Organization
Strong leadership team with very clear Strategic goals
Transformational Projects with a Digital / Technological focus
Facility to work in different Functional Areas / Divisions / Countries
cons: Stress resulting from demanding objectives - but more than compensated with the achievements the bank consistently obtains and the very professional environment

advice: Be more willing to learn and grow. There are too many resources for management to not know what they're doing on what's going on.
pros: Great starting salary and lenient on attendance! They do a lot to make sure employees have a decent work/life balance.
cons: Solicit room for grown but mostly lateral movements, not necessarily promotions. Most of the promotional movements are out of state and require relocation. It would be nicer to see growth within the same location.

pros: Flexible hours with option to periodically work from home, competitive pay and benefits, lots of nice people.  Seems like there is lots of opportunity to advance (e.g. from branches to corporate), transfer and relocate (e.g. Spain).  Seems to be (slowly) moving in the right direction.
cons: Too many hours, it's difficult to move things forward, lots of red tape, some really negative and unprofessional people, lack of clear direction, lack of cooperation amongst departments, lack of resources, lack of common goals.

summary: As a Purchasing Agent, I did a lot of jobs.
advice: Please take into consideration the work load you assign to each of your employees.
pros: The benefits are terrific. The location of good. The pay is competitive. My co-workers were friendly and always helpful. Multiple departments in one building.
cons: You are expected to do any additional jobs they throw at you. When I posted out to a new one-person position, I was told I would do the new job and my existing job.

pros:
- Never ending problems that need to be solved.
- Some of the best people to work with across the world.
cons:
- Senior Management (not as bad as it used to be, but still not good)
- The only thing constant is that nothing is constant.  Maybe a plus for some but it's hard to get your team into a rhythm when process changes at the drop of a hat.

advice: Be coherent with your promise and vison: simple, personal, fair
pros:
The salary
The colleagues 
The name and experience to get
The wide and rich projects you can be involved 
The opportunity to travel and see the different business strategies in all the countries
cons: It’s the opposite of what they promise since the new President Ana Botín arrived. It’s un personal, un fair and really complicated place to work. She made the company a place for her friends and family.

advice: Invest in your people- there’s a lot of give in the incentives and recognition areas. Start with training. If it isn’t feasible to migrate from existing systems to SaaS, the money spent on dummy systems, no matter the cost, could show a significant return. Work with HR and place people you actually trust to manage their areas. There should be room to grow, of course, but it is not where  the primary focus on “development” is likely most appropriate. It was too often that I personally experienced, as well as my peers, employees who would drag teams down and despite best errors, ultimately the manager was left feeling powerless and ineffective. Lastly, less talk, more action- focus on the objective at hand and not every step of the way. If the right leaders are in place, they’ll help everyone win.
pros: Santander is a global bank with a overall good reputation. The customers, for the most part, will say they love their bank, and the bank truly means well in their attitude towards those who bank with them. It is a highly sales driven organization and the monetary incentives are top notch. There is incredible employee recognition for those who generate the most income for the bank.
cons: Execution of all of the above. Though the bank means  well when it comes to delivering excellent service to the customers, branches are often so significantly understaffed to meet the volume of traffic. For some locations this might not be as big of an issue if the bank employee system interfaces are not inconsistent and difficult to navigate. The bank builds and maintains its own applications, making them horribly dated and inefficient especially because their “training” is really no more than a few conference calls and the rest on the new hire. I became accustomed to accepting my customers often seeing significant wait times of up to 25mins for a teller and over an hour and a half for a banker (no exaggeration). No matter intention, how much it is talked about within the company, or how even the best of employees addresses it, this is not delivering positive experiences for the customers. As mentioned above, the sales-driven culture is very much alive and the incentives and recognition awards are no joke. This is fantastic but the way both are structured the employee seeing these rewards are likely not putting the customer, and their coworkers first. In fact most employees feel grossly overworked and undervalued as a direct result. The employees in my group, were often ranked, not by what they brought (or might possibly be capable of bringing) to the table, but by how much money they made the bank. Nothing else. Bankers, and not just my reports, were often known to fight over customers depending on what they walked in for. No true camaraderie. Internal gains aside, the sales process itself is also micromanaged with a focus not on the results, but on HOW they are obtained, which is really not empowering on any level. Finally, it’s hard to make friends, which was a surprisingly challenge for me... and then I learned it was because most people don’t stay very long. I even interacted with a few great people that I thought I have in my corner in my less than 1 year tenure, and they just ended up leaving.  The turnover here is unlike anywhere I have ever worked and it not only takes a toll on employee morale, but also on the customers view of the bank. I was often uncomfortable when told by my customers that I was probably only as permanent as all the others before me that also said they were there to stay. I wanted so much to love this place but I started to really lose myself and the value I knew I had to give. I had to go where I knew it could be utilized.

We know 90% of our customers, so only greeting 20% is not possible. Surveys don’t go out for at least a week after transactions so how would a customer remember if we used their name? So we got worksheets to fill out about what greeting customers should look and sound like. The sheet looked like elementary school homework. When I complained about the ever-changing and ever-growing list of nonsense being heaped upon us, I was told to be a “good company soldier” and was told that I needed to talk to someone about my mental health.

It should be noted that your Business Administration Support Manager started as a CSA and was so bad at her job that her FCs demanded that she no longer be permitted to speak to their respective clients so, on the heels of that, you chose to promote her to management??? And management over the rest of the CSAs, at that??? What on earth were you thinking??? Regardless, the CSAs performance should be measured by the FCs they support and nobody else in regards to the quality of their work and its timeliness. If you want a BASM to be there as a hall monitor to ensure adherence to the time clock and dress code, so be it, but you'd do well to find one who can walk that talk at all times in order to set a less hypocritical standard first, otherwise, you're just sowing the seeds of discontent from day one.

cons: Everything else. Your immediate supervisor, aka Business Administration Support Manager, is as bumbling and inept as they come, so expect to be ineffectively micromanaged at every turn. That is to say when she's actually there. You'll be told that arriving on-time is, in effect, "late" because you have to be "seated with all systems up and ready to go" when the clock strikes 9:00, yet it's not uncommon to see her waddling in to the office in complete disarray well past 9:30, only to immediately come to you and ask to see what work you've completed thus far and, more often than not, whatever you've done will be unsatisfactory in her eyes, regardless of what your Financial Counselors (the advisors in the field you actually support - you know, the ones whose feedback REALLY matters) have to say about it. When you realize that you already know more about the job than she ever will and turn to her immediate supervisor up at HQ to intervene on your behalf, you'll immediately be reprimanded for jumping the chain of command and not working it out with none other than the source of the problem itself, the Business Administration Support Manager. Really? Yes, really. Next thing you know, here come the write-ups, virtually insuring that you're on your way out by way of a fictitious paper trail to justify your termination. What to do, you ask? Well, don't bother going to HR, because they're strictly there to create the illusion that your voice matters and will be heard when, in reality, they're just corporate shills who are not only there to run interference for those you're complaining about, but will turn right around and dime you out to the source despite their insistence that what you say inside their office is "strictly confidential." Right, I'm sure it's pure coincidence how my supervisor was able to recite back to me some direct quotes I'd said in my "confidential" one-on-one meetings with HR when, on her best day, she couldn't string together a coherent message to our team either verbally or over e-mail, let alone the well thought out ones I'd laid out to our in-house HR guy.

Permanently disfunction communication channels make this problem even worse, as managers do not actually read emails or notifications, and immediately start blaming everyone else before understanding the problem.  This company has gone through 3 different CEOs, 4 different CFOs, and 4 different CROs in the past 3 years alone.  What does that tell you about the quality of management selection and the ability of the company to properly guide talent to making the right decisions?  It should be a huge red flag.  Managers at this company are utterly and completely thoughtless.  They try to force their own ideas on the company by promoting and shifting groups without regard to the people those groups contain and end up making previously alright situations into worse ones.  HR is utterly incompetent.  Multiple reports of HR violations go completely unacknowledged and the team members who have to deal with bosses who are completely unreasonable and boderline sexist simply have to keep on dealing with those individuals.  The entire company is clandestine in nature and viciously territorial, which makes it impossible to actually accomplish anything.   The company  has an annual survey, but doesn't actually release results in a text format.  You are verbally told what results are, and verbally told that things will be done about it, but then nothing every actually happens.  There is absolutely ZERO clarity into what it takes to get promoted.  Promotions are almost never announced, so it's impossible to tell who to emulate.  For a "consumer driven technology company" there is almost NO investment in technology on the corporate side.  Servicing is a different, but I have never been at a corporate HQ with such a complete reliance on manual processes and, literally, documents you are supposed to reference in order to figure anything out, most of which are outdate anyway.

advice: Have mercy on everyone and just quit.
pros: The best thing about Santander is that, if you are talented and have a backbone, your time there is likely to be short. Turnover in corporate treasury was nearly 50% in 11 months, and most people hired for their skills leave soon after their one-year anniversary. What remains is the sludge that came in through connections and nepotism.
cons:
A job at Santander bank could mean the end of your career. No one will touch you after this.
The culture is intensely feudal. Self-abasement is expected (picture an army of obsequious sycophants praising spanish royalty for breaking wind). They even have an Orwellian system to track how much each employee participates in the corporate totem-pole rituals. Anyone not enthusiastically participating gets quietly sidelined and will never know why. Needless to say, merit and talent prefer escaping rather than suffocate in the swamp.

Which explains why this is such a poorly run organization. This is the only bank in all of USA that has failed regulatory stress tests three times. A notorious record in itself. The reasons have always been serious shortcomings in risk management and basic operations. No wonder why many employees are leary of opening accounts there despite pressure from management. Even good, conscientious employees who go above and beyond to fix problems outside their job description soon realize that it's like finding a roach - there's more where they came from, never just one. Some of the dysfunctionality arises from a bizzarre IT setup - PRODUBAN and ISBAN, two subsidiaries of the Madrid parent company that almost exclusively provide IT services to the US bank subsidiary. The purpose appears to be to find ways around the US regulators' will, and secretly control the US bank.

If you have any sort of integrity and stand up to pressure to bend rules and laws (which executives themselves brazenly do), they will trap you like a fish in their net of compliance policies. They ruthlessly enforce their policies on employees, while executives go scot-free for far worse conduct.

Management pads their own bonuses while cutting bonuses for the rank and file, while cynically telling staff the opposite, claiming that they are making a sacrifice! The branch staff themselves can be seen carrying placards on the street to protest unfair pay and labor practices.

They systematically defraud new hires who have a discretionary bonus in their offer with a bait and switch. Towards the end of the year, they will put a new agreement in front of you and tell you that your bonus will be zero unless you sign it. The agreement materially changes the terms of the offer letter based on which you took the job. If you accept a job here, be ready to get a zero bonus, even if it was multiple times your base pay. Be forewarned!

cons:
I have never worked in a business environment that was so grim and depressing. A very sharp contrast from the previous employer. A few bullet points about this experience:

- Santander cancelled access to the building's cafeteria and all employees have to be cramped in small break rooms.
- Right off the bat the company fired one out of every four employees and their work spread among the rest, substantially increasing the work load.
- Bonuses were cut by 75% and management went to great lengths in finding little details in order not to pay it.
- The only meetings we had with the new management were always filled with threats and their favorite go to phrase "if you don't like it, you can always leave".
- We were required to work every other Saturday and calling sick on that day (as oppose to a week day) was considered a "no show".
- The new management was very abusive in their communications, demanding people to work overtime and publicly chastising those who didn't.
- Every week people were quitting their jobs because of the working conditions.
- I personally approach my manager and two of the directors to bring this sudden change and was dismissed with their favorite line "if you don't like it, you can leave anytime".
- The working culture was to collect money at any cost and whatever means necessary.

Overall Santander brought a worsening of the working conditions; a reduction in pay and increased in work; and management that was abusive and unresponsive to even some basic  good practices of a working environment.

Even our customers noticed this sudden change and started referring to Santander as "Satan-der" for how abusive their collections practices became. 

Shortly after I found a new job and left, they closed the office and laid off everybody.

In all my years doing work inside and outside of the financial system, Santander takes the gold medal as the most abusive company I've ever worked for.

4) Their implementation of forced calls through a queue ruined the experience for a lot of dealers. All the sales guys are on a plan and must perform, but more often than not, someone else in the group would get the call and offer money that would come out of my pocket without asking first, or at the very least, to follow-up and advise what had taken place.
5) Management was very unprofessional in their communications to the floor. Often threats were made in e-mails that left everyone with a sense of discomfort, like someone was holding a gun to your head.
6) Although they pay overtime, you are pretty much forced to work 9+ hrs per day and mandatory Saturdays, even if it wasn't part of your schedule. Management frowned upon those that may have had other obligations.....like a life.
7) The pay is not that great (below average) and they basically want you to catch up the crappy base with OT. The commission structure is also pretty bad and almost impossible to track with any kind of consistency.
8) The fact that there are 7 major drawbacks should be enough for anyone to determine how this company operates....very unethically.
